meta.blurb: Wren Ashby has one second to stop her aunt's matchmaking, so she points at the nearest man in the café. Kit, the ferry mechanic, plays along. Their rules fit on a napkin. Their feelings do not.
meta.bible: Wren Ashby: 29, a children's book illustrator in Salt Cove, warm, funny, shy about her work, tends to say yes to everyone. Kit Navarro: 31, the mechanic who keeps the little ferry Gannet running, quiet, dry humour, hums while he works, never says what he feels; his fiancée Dana left him two years ago. Leo: Kit's nephew, 8, lives with Kit, loves dragons and bikes. Aunt Dot: Dorothy Ashby, 70s, Wren's aunt, chairs the Lantern Fair, cannot stop matchmaking, wise and sly. Dana: Kit's ex, who comes back for one weekend. Marta: Wren's best friend, runs the bookshop. Mr Pell: owns Pell's Café, loves gossip. Ms Halden: an editor at Halden and Moss in Barrowfield. Salt Cove: a small seaside town. Barrowfield: the big city, two hours away by train. Pell's Café: where it starts. Lantern Fair: the town's night in six weeks, when paper lanterns are floated on the bay. The Sleepy Lighthouse: Wren's current picture book. Gannet: the ferry. The napkin rules: no real kissing except in public when needed; no lying to Leo; no feelings; it ends the day after the Lantern Fair. Ending: Wren takes the Halden job but works from Salt Cove; Kit and Wren are truly together; the napkin is framed at Pell's Café. Voice and tone: warm, light, funny, a slow-burning pretend romance with real feeling underneath; clean, no bad language. Full-length facts: Wren's cat is Pickle, a fat grey cat. Wren lives in a small flat above the sail-maker's shop on Gull Lane. The Sleepy Lighthouse is about Percy, a round lighthouse who keeps falling asleep. Dr Ruiz: the new vet, kind and shy, with a spaniel called Biscuit; he and Marta slowly fall for each other. Rose Cottage: Aunt Dot's house, with a yellow door and a garden full of roses. Rosa: Kit's sister, who works on a research ship for the year and calls Leo on a tablet. Mrs Tully: Leo's teacher at Salt Cove School. Mrs Abara: sells cheese at the Saturday market on the quay. Marram: the village across the bay where the Gannet sails. Kit lives in a blue-doored house on Anchor Lane beside the ferry shed; the loft above the shed has a big window to the sea and later becomes Wren's studio. Dana's cousin Felix marries in Salt Cove on the weekend Dana comes back, with a party in the Anchor Hall. Dana left two years ago for a job in the city and waited a year for Kit to ask her to stay; he never did. Aunt Dot's old love was Henry Marsh, who asked her to sail away with him; she was too frightened to say yes, and she kept his letters in a shoebox. The napkin rules in order: one, no feelings; two, no lying to Leo; three, kisses only in public and only when needed; four, it all ends the day after the Lantern Fair. Kit keeps the napkin in his shirt pocket. Kit's father kept the Gannet for thirty years and now lives on the south coast and sends postcards. Hazel is Felix's bride. Leo's dragons include Soot (grumpy), Ember (brave) and Pudding (purple, afraid of thunder); Dana gave Leo a glass dragon. Kit gives Wren a brass washer from the Gannet's first engine for luck. Rule five, made at the lantern painting: no peeking at each other's wishes until the night of the fair; Kit's wish reads Ask her to stay and Wren's reads Be brave enough to ask. Mr Pell's lantern is a giant cinnamon bun. Marta and Dr Ruiz end up together; Marta wins her cinnamon-bun bet. The fair is on a Saturday night six weeks after the café scene. Wren's interview is on the Friday a week before the fair; Ms Halden wants an answer by the next Friday.

beats.scene: Wren draws foxes and owls at a window table in a seaside café.
beats.summary: Wren Ashby draws at her usual table in Pell's Café in the seaside town of Salt Cove.

beats.scene: A drawing of a round lighthouse in a nightcap lies in the sketchbook.
beats.summary: Her new book is about Percy, a lighthouse who keeps falling asleep, and the deadline is close.

beats.scene: Mr Pell sets a cup of tea and a bun beside Wren's sketchbook.
beats.summary: Mr Pell brings her usual tea and a bun, along with the morning's gossip.

beats.scene: Wren sits buried under a knitting bag, a ladder and a cake tin.
beats.summary: Wren cannot say no: she has agreed to every club, errand and favour in town.

beats.scene: An older woman in a bright scarf waves a paper list at Wren.
beats.summary: Aunt Dot sweeps into the café with a list in her hand and a gleam in her eye.

beats.scene: Aunt Dot reads names from a long list while Wren stares at her tea.
beats.summary: Dot reads out her list of six suitable young men, with notes on each.

beats.scene: Aunt Dot points at the café clock while Wren looks horrified.
beats.summary: Dot has booked a dinner for Wren with the new vet tonight at seven.

beats.scene: Wren counts excuses on her fingers while Aunt Dot shakes her head.
beats.summary: Wren tries a deadline, a headache and a cat, and Dot has an answer for each.

beats.scene: Dot taps her wristwatch and smiles while Wren glances toward the door.
beats.summary: Dot says she will walk Wren to the restaurant herself, so Wren has one second to find a way out.

beats.scene: A brass bell above the café door swings as someone steps inside.
beats.summary: The café bell rings, and Wren looks up at the door, desperate for any escape.

beats.scene: A broad-shouldered man in a stained work shirt walks through the café door.
beats.summary: Kit Navarro, the ferry mechanic, walks in with oil on his hands to order coffee.

beats.scene: Wren stares across the busy café at the man standing at the counter.
beats.summary: Wren knows Kit only by sight, as the quiet man who hums over engines.

beats.scene: Wren points straight at Kit while Aunt Dot's mouth drops open.
beats.summary: Wren blurts out that she is already seeing someone, and points at Kit.

beats.scene: Kit stands frozen at the counter holding a coin in mid-air.
beats.summary: Kit freezes at the counter while the whole café stares at him.

beats.scene: Kit puts a hand on Wren's shoulder and gives a slow smile.
beats.summary: Kit sees Wren's frightened face, then smiles slowly and plays along.

beats.scene: Aunt Dot claps her hands while Wren and Kit stand stiffly side by side.
beats.summary: Dot is delighted and asks how long this has been going on; Kit says a few weeks.

beats.scene: Aunt Dot holds a phone to her ear, beaming, while Wren stares in disbelief.
beats.summary: Dot cheerfully phones Dr Ruiz and cancels the dinner.

beats.scene: Aunt Dot writes in a red notebook and points at a calendar.
beats.summary: Dot invites them to Sunday lunch and says the whole town will meet Kit at the Lantern Fair in six weeks.

beats.scene: Aunt Dot sails out of the café while Mr Pell winks.
beats.summary: Dot leaves, glowing, and Mr Pell winks and says the coffee is on the house.

beats.scene: Wren and Kit stand outside the café beside a bicycle rack.
beats.summary: Outside, Wren apologises, and Kit is annoyed but amused.

beats.scene: Kit rubs his forehead on the pavement while gulls wheel overhead.
beats.summary: Kit points out that Dot will tell the whole town by noon.

beats.scene: Kit leans on a low harbour wall and looks out across the bay.
beats.summary: Kit admits the town has pitied him since his fiancée left.

beats.scene: Kit counts on his fingers while Wren listens with wide eyes.
beats.summary: Kit suggests they pretend until the Lantern Fair and then end it quietly.

beats.scene: Wren hesitates, twisting the strap of her bag.
beats.summary: Wren agrees, because Dot will finally stop and because Kit is kind about it.

beats.scene: Mr Pell brings a pen and a paper napkin to a small corner table.
beats.summary: They agree they need rules, and Mr Pell, pretending not to listen, brings a napkin and a pen.

beats.scene: Kit writes in careful capital letters on a white paper napkin.
beats.summary: Rule one: no feelings.

beats.scene: Kit's pen pauses above the napkin as he talks about a small boy.
beats.summary: Rule two: no lying to Leo. Kit explains that his nephew Leo, eight, lives with him.

beats.scene: Wren raises her eyebrows as Kit writes a third rule on the napkin.
beats.summary: Rule three: kisses only in public, and only when needed.

beats.scene: Wren draws a tiny dragon on the napkin beside four rules.
beats.summary: Rule four: it ends the day after the Lantern Fair. They sign, and Wren draws a dragon.

beats.scene: Kit folds the napkin and slips it into his shirt pocket.
beats.summary: Kit folds the napkin into his shirt pocket and they shake hands on the deal.

beats.scene: Marta laughs behind a counter of books while Wren covers her face.
beats.summary: Wren tells her best friend Marta everything, and Marta laughs until she cries.

beats.scene: Marta presses a paperback into Wren's hands among tall shelves.
beats.summary: Marta warns that every book she sells with this plan ends in love, and Wren says this is real life.

beats.scene: Wren lies awake with a fat grey cat curled on her pillow.
beats.summary: That night Wren lies awake beside her cat, wondering what she has done.

beats.scene: Wren's phone glows on a pillow with a long list of messages.
beats.summary: Kit and Wren swap numbers and messages, learning each other's favourite things so their story will match.

beats.scene: Wren and Kit walk up a lane toward a house with a yellow door.
beats.summary: On Sunday Wren and Kit walk to Rose Cottage, with a gap between them wide enough for a goat.

beats.scene: A big table with a roast chicken, and Aunt Dot leaning forward.
beats.summary: At lunch, Dot asks how they met, and they have not planned a story.

beats.scene: Kit tells a story with his hands while everyone laughs.
beats.summary: Kit invents a funny story: Wren fell off the jetty, and he fished her out.

beats.scene: Wren waves her arms wildly while Kit watches with one eyebrow raised.
beats.summary: Wren adds details that do not match: a green jetty, freezing water and a fishing net.

beats.scene: Marta chokes on her tea while Aunt Dot smiles knowingly.
beats.summary: Marta chokes on her tea, and Dot gives a small, knowing smile.

beats.scene: Wren dries a plate beside Aunt Dot at a sunny kitchen sink.
beats.summary: Washing up, Dot tells Wren that Kit is a good man who has been hurt, and Wren feels guilty.

beats.scene: Wren reads a message on her phone beside a cup of tea.
beats.summary: On Monday Kit messages Wren: Leo wants to meet her before anyone tells him a story.

beats.scene: A small house with a blue door stands beside a tall ferry shed.
beats.summary: Wren goes to Kit's house on Anchor Lane, with its blue door and a dragon on the doormat.

beats.scene: A small boy with a toy dragon looks up at a woman.
beats.summary: Leo meets Wren and asks if she is Kit's girlfriend.

beats.scene: Wren kneels to Leo's height and speaks gently while Kit watches.
beats.summary: Wren answers honestly: she is Kit's friend and will be around a lot for a while.

beats.scene: A bedroom shelf crowded with dragons of every colour and size.
beats.summary: Leo shows Wren his forty-one dragons, each with a name and a story.

beats.scene: Wren draws a round green dragon while Leo watches with folded arms.
beats.summary: Leo asks Wren to draw a dragon, and he has opinions about it.

beats.scene: Wren adds sharp teeth and a curl of smoke to the dragon drawing.
beats.summary: Wren redraws the dragon with a reason for its fire, and Leo approves.

beats.scene: A tablet shows a smiling woman on a ship's deck, birds behind her.
beats.summary: Rosa, Kit's sister, calls from her research ship; she knows the truth and laughs.

beats.scene: Kit stirs a pot at the stove while Leo sets plates on a table.
beats.summary: Kit makes fish fingers and peas, and Wren stays for dinner and laughs a lot.

beats.scene: A laptop glows with an email while a sketch lies unfinished.
beats.summary: That night, Wren's editor Ms Halden emails: she wants Wren to come for a job interview in Barrowfield.

beats.scene: Wren reads a laptop in bed at dawn, a grey cat on her knee.
beats.summary: At dawn Wren rereads the email: Halden and Moss is the publisher she has dreamed of since she was a girl.

beats.scene: Wren stands at her window looking at grey water and a long road.
beats.summary: Wren is thrilled and frightened at once, because a job in Barrowfield would mean leaving Salt Cove.

beats.scene: Marta hugs Wren in the bookshop doorway with a book clutched to her chest.
beats.summary: Wren tells Marta about the email, and Marta says she must go to the interview.

beats.scene: Wren carries a flask of tea along a rainy jetty to a ferry.
beats.summary: Wren brings tea to Kit while he repairs the ferry in the rain, and the town watches.

beats.scene: Kit looks up from an open engine with rain running down his face.
beats.summary: Kit is so surprised by the tea that he forgets to speak, then thanks her quietly.

beats.scene: Kit points to a brass part inside the engine while Wren leans in close.
beats.summary: Wren asks about the engine, and Kit explains for ten minutes and forgets to be shy.

beats.scene: Mr Pell leans over the counter whispering to a row of eager customers.
beats.summary: By lunchtime Mr Pell has told everyone that Wren carried tea to Kit in the rain.

beats.scene: Wren holds a ringing phone away from her ear in a bright kitchen.
beats.summary: Dot phones, delighted, to say she has heard about the tea.

beats.scene: A phone screen shows a short message from Kit and a smiling face.
beats.summary: Kit texts to thank her for the tea and suggests they practise at the Saturday market.

beats.scene: A tiny ferry sails across the margin of a drawing of a round lighthouse.
beats.summary: That night Wren draws, and a tiny ferry appears in the margin of Percy's page.

beats.scene: Colourful market stalls line the quay under bright striped awnings.
beats.summary: On Saturday the market fills the quay, and Wren finds Kit waiting by the fruit stall, nervous.

beats.scene: Wren and Kit hold hands stiffly among the market stalls.
beats.summary: They practise holding hands at the market, and both are awkward.

beats.scene: A woman behind a cheese stall grins and points a cheese knife at them.
beats.summary: Mrs Abara at the cheese stall says they hold hands like two people carrying a wardrobe.

beats.scene: Marta waves from a crowded bookstall and shows how to walk in step.
beats.summary: Marta tells them to relax their shoulders and walk in step.

beats.scene: Wren and Kit walk side by side past market stalls, laughing, hands loosely linked.
beats.summary: They try again, laugh, and it gets easier.

beats.scene: Mr Pell cheers behind a bun stall as Kit kisses Wren's cheek.
beats.summary: Kit kisses Wren on the cheek for the crowd, and both are shaken.

beats.scene: Kit stares at a cabbage with a red face while Wren touches her cheek.
beats.summary: Both are shaken: Wren's cheek burns and Kit stares hard at a cabbage.

beats.scene: Kit hands Wren a paper cone of pink flowers at a flower stall.
beats.summary: Kit buys Wren sweet peas without thinking, then says it is only for the act.

beats.scene: Kit kneels under a wobbly cheese stall, tightening a bolt, humming.
beats.summary: Kit fixes a wobbling stall without being asked, humming, and Wren notices the hum.

beats.scene: Wren sketches a man humming beside an engine at a kitchen table.
beats.summary: That night Wren sketches Kit from memory, with his hum drawn as curling lines.

beats.scene: Leo bounces into the café waving a wooden sword, with Kit behind him.
beats.summary: On Sunday Leo bursts into Pell's Café with Kit, asking if his dragon is finished.

beats.scene: Kit holds a sketchbook page and looks at it quietly.
beats.summary: Kit sees the sketch of himself, says nobody has ever drawn him and asks to keep it.

beats.scene: Leo draws a dragon on a paper placemat while Kit speaks quietly to Wren.
beats.summary: Kit says he hums when he is content, and that Dana used to say it drove her mad.

beats.scene: Kit folds a drawing carefully into his shirt pocket.
beats.summary: Wren gives Kit the drawing, and he folds it into his pocket beside the napkin.

beats.scene: Marta stands among shelves of books with her arms folded.
beats.summary: Marta, in the bookshop, tells Wren she is a terrible actress and suspects the romance is not pretend.

beats.scene: Marta and Wren shake hands over a bookshop counter, both grinning.
beats.summary: Marta bets Wren a cinnamon bun every Friday for a year that the pretending will turn real.

beats.scene: Kit and Wren stand at the wheel of a small ferry on blue water.
beats.summary: Kit teaches Wren to steer the ferry Gannet across the bay.

beats.scene: Kit points at pale ripples on the water as the ferry glides past rocks.
beats.summary: Kit teaches her to read the water: where the tide runs deep and where the rocks lie.

beats.scene: The ferry glides home across a rosy bay with only two people aboard.
beats.summary: No one is watching, yet they stand close and keep talking; both forget they are pretending.

beats.scene: Two people sit on a harbour wall at night under bright stars.
beats.summary: After tying up the ferry they sit on the harbour wall under the stars and talk late.

beats.scene: Kit looks at the black water and points toward the ferry shed.
beats.summary: Kit tells her his father kept the Gannet before him and taught him every bolt.

beats.scene: A young girl draws at a kitchen table under a warm lamp.
beats.summary: Wren tells how she spent childhood summers drawing at Dot's kitchen table while her parents moved for work.

beats.scene: Kit throws a pebble into dark water and rings spread outward.
beats.summary: Kit says it is easier not to ask people to stay, and Wren says she cannot say no to anyone.

beats.scene: A church clock tower shows midnight above dark rooftops.
beats.summary: The church clock strikes midnight, and they realise how late it is.

beats.scene: Kit drapes his jacket over Wren's shoulders under a streetlamp.
beats.summary: Kit lends Wren his jacket and walks her home; they hold hands the whole way without noticing.

beats.scene: Wren wakes with sunlight on her face and a grey cat on her chest.
beats.summary: Wren wakes, sees Kit's jacket on her chair and tells herself rule one still applies.

beats.scene: Aunt Dot taps a long list at a committee table crowded with paper lanterns.
beats.summary: Dot gives Wren and Kit jobs for the Lantern Fair: painting lanterns and mending frames.

beats.scene: Wren reads a message on her phone with a worried frown.
beats.summary: Kit messages that Dana is coming back for the weekend, for her cousin's wedding.

beats.scene: Wren holds a phone to her ear, the dark sea in her window.
beats.summary: Wren phones to say she will be there; Kit admits he has not seen Dana for two years.

beats.scene: A woman in a smart coat stands in the café doorway looking at Kit.
beats.summary: On Friday Dana, Kit's old fiancée, walks into Pell's Café with a suitcase.

beats.scene: Mr Pell drops a teaspoon while the whole café stares at the doorway.
beats.summary: The café falls quiet as everyone recognises Dana.

beats.scene: Kit stands slowly from the table, his hands open at his sides.
beats.summary: Kit stands up slowly, and Dana says his name very softly.

beats.scene: Kit puts an arm around Wren while a stylish woman stares.
beats.summary: Kit introduces Wren as his girlfriend in front of Dana.

beats.scene: Dana smiles politely and holds out a gloved hand to Wren.
beats.summary: Dana is surprised but gracious, and congratulates them, though something sad crosses her face.

beats.scene: A small boy in a school jumper looks at a woman with a gift.
beats.summary: Dana meets Leo at the school gate with a glass dragon, and Leo is polite but wary.

beats.scene: Dana holds out a cream-coloured invitation card to Kit and Wren.
beats.summary: Dana invites them to the wedding on Saturday and the party afterwards in the Anchor Hall.

beats.scene: Dana speaks quietly to Wren beside a bookshop window.
beats.summary: Dana finds Wren alone in the bookshop and says Kit never says what he really feels.

beats.scene: Dana looks out of the bookshop window at the grey harbour.
beats.summary: Dana says she took a job far away and waited a year for Kit to ask her to stay; he never did.

beats.scene: Wren's hands tremble on a book while Dana touches her arm.
beats.summary: Wren defends Kit; Dana says he cares more than anyone but cannot say it, and tells her not to wait.

beats.scene: Wren walks alone along the shore at low tide, shoes in hand.
beats.summary: Wren walks the shore alone and wonders why a pretend romance should hurt.

beats.scene: Wren and Kit face each other across a quiet kitchen under one lamp.
beats.summary: That evening Wren goes to Kit's kitchen and asks why he never talks about feelings.

beats.scene: Kit stands with folded arms beside the kettle, his face closed.
beats.summary: Kit goes stiff and says feelings are covered by rule one, so they need not talk.

beats.scene: Wren holds out her hands while Kit turns toward the dark window.
beats.summary: Wren says Dana told her about waiting a year; Kit says Dana had no right.

beats.scene: Wren and Kit stand silent on either side of a kitchen table.
beats.summary: They argue in whispers, then both say sorry, and the silence is worse.

beats.scene: A bicycle lies on wet flagstones in a dark yard, one wheel bent.
beats.summary: A crash and a wail in the yard: Leo has fallen off his bike.

beats.scene: Kit kneels on wet stones and checks Leo's grazed knee.
beats.summary: Kit comforts Leo with a gentleness Wren has never seen, and words pour out of him.

beats.scene: A child's broken bicycle lies on a garage floor with tools around it.
beats.summary: Next morning Wren, Kit and Leo mend the bike together in the garage.

beats.scene: Wren holds a bicycle wheel while Kit tightens a bolt and Leo passes tools.
beats.summary: They work like a team, and for a few minutes it feels like a family.

beats.scene: Leo looks up from the bicycle with a serious face, holding a spanner.
beats.summary: Leo asks Wren if she will go away like Dana did, and she answers as honestly as she can.

beats.scene: Leo rides a mended bike down Anchor Lane under dark purple clouds.
beats.summary: The bike is mended and Leo rides it down the lane while dark clouds gather over the bay.

beats.scene: Marta fastens the last button on a blue dress in a small flat.
beats.summary: Marta helps Wren dress for the wedding and says Kit is in serious trouble.

beats.scene: Kit in a dark suit stands at the foot of narrow stairs, staring upward.
beats.summary: Kit, in a dark suit, forgets how to speak when he sees Wren, and gives her a bun.

beats.scene: Guests fill a small stone chapel decked with white flowers.
beats.summary: In the small chapel, Felix and Hazel marry, and half the town cries.

beats.scene: Mr Pell holds up a camera as confetti swirls around Wren and Kit.
beats.summary: On the chapel steps Mr Pell insists on a photograph of Wren and Kit in the falling confetti.

beats.scene: Strings of lanterns hang above long tables heaped with cake in a lively hall.
beats.summary: At the party in the Anchor Hall there is a band, a huge cake and a whole town watching.

beats.scene: Across a crowded hall, Dana raises a glass toward Kit.
beats.summary: Across the hall Dana raises her glass to Kit, and Wren takes his hand.

beats.scene: The fiddle band plays while Mr Pell waves Wren and Kit onto the floor.
beats.summary: The band plays a slow waltz, and Mr Pell announces that the happy couple will lead the dance.

beats.scene: Wren and Kit turn slowly under strings of lanterns while the crowd fades.
beats.summary: They dance; Kit is clumsy at first and then not, and the room fades away.

beats.scene: The hall doors bang open in a gust of wind as lightning flashes.
beats.summary: As the dance ends, thunder rolls and the doors bang open: the storm has arrived.

beats.scene: Two people run through heavy rain holding their coats over their heads.
beats.summary: They run through the storm to fetch Leo from Dot's, and the streetlamps go out.

beats.scene: Leo sits wrapped in a blanket in a dark hall, eyes shining.
beats.summary: They reach the blue door soaked; Leo wakes and is thrilled that the power is out.

beats.scene: Candles flicker on a dark kitchen table beside a small camping stove.
beats.summary: With the power out, Kit lights a camping stove and they decide to make soup.

beats.scene: Wren stirs a pot while Kit chops onions, both laughing in candlelight.
beats.summary: They cook together in the candlelight, bumping elbows and laughing.

beats.scene: Three bowls of soup steam on a kitchen table in candlelight.
beats.summary: They eat soup by candlelight, and Leo tells a story about a dragon afraid of thunder.

beats.scene: Leo sleeps on a sofa under a blanket, a toy dragon under his chin.
beats.summary: Leo falls asleep on the sofa, and Kit tucks a blanket over him.

beats.scene: Kit sits at the kitchen table with both hands around a mug.
beats.summary: Quietly, Kit tells Wren about the morning Dana left: he stood on the quay and watched the Gannet carry her away.

beats.scene: Wren reaches across the table and rests her hand over Kit's.
beats.summary: Wren takes his hand and asks what he would have said that morning; he says stay.

beats.scene: Kit's thumb brushes a smudge of soup from Wren's cheek in candlelight.
beats.summary: Kit wipes a smudge of soup from Wren's cheek, and his hand stays; neither of them moves.

beats.scene: Two people stand very close in a dim kitchen, faces almost touching.
beats.summary: They stand up, the table no longer between them, and almost kiss.

beats.scene: Kit holds a single candle in a doorway as Wren walks away.
beats.summary: Wren whispers “rules” and Kit steps back; she walks home alone in the thinning rain.

beats.scene: Planks and branches lie scattered along a beach after a storm, with gulls wheeling.
beats.summary: Next morning the storm has washed a long mountain of driftwood onto the beach.

beats.scene: Kit and Dana stand on the quay beside the ferry, speaking quietly.
beats.summary: Dana leaves on the Gannet; Kit speaks to her at length, and Wren watches from far away.

beats.scene: Kit walks slowly along the quay toward Wren with his hands in his pockets.
beats.summary: Kit tells Wren he said sorry to Dana, two years late, and she forgave him.

beats.scene: Wren talks across a counter of books while Marta listens closely.
beats.summary: Wren admits to Marta that her feelings for Kit are real.

beats.scene: Marta takes Wren's hands across a bookshop counter while a customer waits.
beats.summary: Marta says Wren must tell Kit; Wren says rule one, and she is afraid of losing him.

beats.scene: Kit and Leo drag silvery planks of driftwood up the beach.
beats.summary: Kit and Leo gather the best driftwood for a secret project, and Leo keeps the secret for almost an hour.

beats.scene: Kit sands a small driftwood desk in a lamplit workshop.
beats.summary: Kit builds Wren a small desk from driftwood, made for the real her.

beats.scene: Wren draws a huge dragon on a whiteboard while children shout suggestions.
beats.summary: Wren draws a dragon on the whiteboard while the children shout what it needs.

beats.scene: Kit stands at the back of the hall behind stacked chairs, arms folded, smiling.

beats.scene: Wren and Kit sit on a harbour bench with a laptop between them.

A1A2: Every morning, Wren drew little animals at her table in Pell's Café.
Her new book was about a lighthouse who kept falling asleep.
Mr Pell brought her tea and a bun, as he did every day.
Wren could not say no, so she was always busy.
Aunt Dot came in with a bright scarf and a paper list.
Dot had a list of six nice young men for Wren.
Dot had planned a dinner with the new vet for tonight.
Wren said she was busy, but Dot would not listen.
Dot said she would walk Wren to dinner herself.
Just then, the café door opened and the bell rang.
Kit, the ferry mechanic, came in with oil on his hands.
Wren knew him a little, but they had never really talked.
Wren jumped up, pointed at Kit and cried, “I'm seeing him!”
Kit stood still, and the whole café looked at him.
Kit saw her scared face, and then he smiled slowly.
Dot clapped her hands with joy and asked how long.
Dot called the vet and cancelled the dinner right away.
Dot asked them to Sunday lunch at her house.
Dot left the café, smiling, and Mr Pell winked.
Outside the café, Wren said sorry again and again.
Kit said her aunt would tell the whole town by noon.
People had felt sorry for Kit since his fiancée left.
Kit said, “Let's pretend until the Lantern Fair.”
Wren thought for a minute and then, as always, said yes.
They sat at a small table to make rules.
Rule one was simple: no feelings, for either of them.
Rule two said that nobody could ever lie to Leo.
Rule three was to kiss only in public, and only when needed.
Rule four said it would end the day after the fair.
Kit put the paper in his pocket, and they shook hands.
Wren told her friend Marta, who laughed and laughed.
Marta said that stories like this usually end in love.
That night Wren could not sleep, and her cat watched her.
Kit and Wren sent texts about their favourite things.
On Sunday, they walked to Aunt Dot's house together.
At lunch, Dot asked, “How did you two meet?”
Kit said that Wren fell into the sea and he saved her.
Wren added her own details, and they did not match.
Marta spilled her tea, and Dot smiled to herself.

Leo looked up and asked, “Are you Kit's girlfriend?”

Leo showed her his dragons, and each one had a name.
Leo asked Wren to draw a dragon for him.
Wren drew new teeth, and Leo said it was perfect.
Leo's mother called from a ship and waved at Wren.
Wren stayed for dinner, and Leo talked the whole time.
An email came from Ms Halden, who wanted to meet Wren.
Wren read the email again, and her hands shook.
A job in the city meant leaving Salt Cove.
Wren told Marta, who said, “You must go!”
Wren took hot tea to Kit in the rain.
Kit looked up, surprised, and said a quiet thank you.
Wren asked about the engine, and Kit talked and talked.
By lunch, everyone in town knew about the tea.
Aunt Dot called her, very happy about the tea.
Kit sent a message to thank her for the tea.
That night, Wren drew a tiny ferry beside Percy.
On Saturday, the market was busy, and everyone was looking.
They tried to hold hands, but it felt strange.
Mrs Abara at the cheese stall laughed at their stiff hands.
Marta told them to relax and walk in step.
They tried again, and this time it felt easier.
Kit kissed Wren's cheek, and the crowd cheered loudly.
Wren's face felt hot, and Kit looked at a cabbage.

Kit fixed a shaky stall and hummed a quiet tune.
That night, Wren drew Kit as he hummed.
On Sunday, Leo ran into the café with Kit.
Kit looked at the drawing and said, “Nobody ever drew me.”
Kit said he hummed when he felt happy and calm.
Wren gave him the drawing, and he put it away.
Marta said, “You are a very bad actress.”
Marta made a bet about a bun, and Wren agreed.
Kit let Wren steer the little ferry across the bay.
Kit showed her where the water was deep and safe.
Nobody was watching, but they stood close anyway.
They sat on the harbour wall under the stars.
Kit said his father had fixed the Gannet before him.
Wren told him she drew at Dot's table as a girl.
Kit said it was easier not to ask people to stay.
The church clock rang twelve times, and they jumped.
Kit lent Wren his jacket and walked her home.
Wren woke up and saw Kit's jacket on her chair.
Dot gave them both jobs for the Lantern Fair.
Kit sent a message: Dana was coming back for a weekend.
Wren said she would stand beside Kit the whole weekend.
A woman in a smart coat stood at the café door.
Everyone in the café stopped and stared at Dana.
Kit stood up slowly, and Dana said his name.
Kit put an arm around Wren and said, “This is my girlfriend.”
Dana was surprised, but she smiled and said hello.
Dana had brought Leo a dragon from the north.
Dana asked them both to come to the wedding.
Dana said that Kit never said what he felt.
Dana said she waited a year for Kit to ask her to stay.
Dana said, “Don't wait for him like I did.”
Wren walked alone by the sea, with a heavy heart.
That evening, Wren went to Kit's kitchen with a question.
Kit went stiff and said that feelings were not part of the deal.
Wren said that Dana had told her everything, and Kit looked hurt.
They both said sorry, and then nobody spoke.
Suddenly, they heard a crash and a loud cry outside.
Kit sat beside Leo and looked at his knee gently.
On Saturday morning, they all fixed the bike together.
They worked well together, almost like a real family.
Leo asked, “Will you go away like Dana did?”
Leo rode the bike down the lane, and dark clouds came.
Marta helped Wren put on her best blue dress.
Kit saw Wren in her dress and forgot every word.
Felix married his bride in the small stone chapel.
Mr Pell took a photo of them outside the chapel.
At the party, there was music, cake and dancing.
Dana raised her glass to Kit across the room.

When the song ended, thunder shook the hall.
They ran through the rain to get Leo from Dot's.
Leo woke up and loved the dark, stormy night.

They cooked together, and their elbows kept bumping.
They ate hot soup, and Leo told a story about dragons.
Leo fell asleep on the sofa with his dragon.
Kit told Wren about the day Dana left.
Wren held his hand and asked what he wanted to say.
Kit touched her cheek, and neither of them moved.
They moved closer, and their faces were almost touching.
Wren whispered one word, “Rules,” and Kit stepped back.
After the storm, the beach was covered with wood.
Dana left on the ferry, and Kit spoke to her.
Kit told Wren he had said sorry to Dana.
Wren told Marta that her feelings for Kit were real.
Marta said to tell him, but Wren was too afraid.

After school, Wren told Kit about her job interview.
Kit said he was happy for her, but he looked sad.
Wren waited for Kit to say stay, but he did not.
Dot said Kit looked at Wren like a lighthouse.
In the town hall, everyone painted paper lanterns for the fair.
Dr Ruiz came with his dog and sat next to Marta.
Mr Pell painted his lantern like a big cinnamon bun.
Wren and Kit each painted a secret wish inside a lantern.
They promised not to look at each other's wishes.
Kit tested a lantern raft in the water, and it floated.
Kit gave her a small brass ring for luck.

She tried to imagine life in the city, without the sea.
At dawn, Wren waited for her train and held the lucky charm.
The train ran past green fields toward a grey city.
The city was loud, and nobody looked at Wren.
The publishing house was in a very tall glass building.
Wren saw her favourite childhood books on the wall.
Ms Halden smiled and showed Wren her own drawings.
Ms Halden said Wren's pictures were kind and funny.
Ms Halden offered Wren a job right then and there.
Ms Halden asked for her answer in one week.
Wren had lunch alone and thought about Kit.
Wren called Marta and said, “They offered me the job.”
On the train home, rain fell against the window.

Kit stood on the platform with a big umbrella.
Kit held the umbrella over her and took her bag.
At last Kit asked, “How did it go?”
Wren said Ms Halden liked her work and offered a job.
Wren said she did not know and needed to think.
Kit said, “I would never ask you to stay.”

Wren stood up and said, “Maybe it was all pretend.”

Leo came to her door with a drawing of them.

Leo took her hand and said, “Come with me.”

Wren sat at the desk and wrote an email to Ms Halden.
Ms Halden wrote back quickly and said yes.

Wren hurried along the beach, looking for Kit everywhere.

B1B2: Every morning Wren Ashby carried her sketchbook to the same window table in Pell's Café. Salt Cove was a small town by the sea, and she had never wanted to live anywhere else.
Her new picture book, The Sleepy Lighthouse, was about a lighthouse called Percy who kept falling asleep on the job. The pictures were nearly finished, but the last six were due in a month.
Mr Pell, who owned the café, brought her tea and a cinnamon bun without being asked. He also brought the morning gossip, which in Salt Cove was served with everything.
Wren had one great weakness, which was that she could not say no to anyone. Over the years she had agreed to run the raffle, paint the fence and knit forty scarves for charity.
At nine the café door swung open and Aunt Dot swept in, wearing a bright scarf and carrying a sheet of paper. Wren knew that look, and her heart sank right down into her shoes.
Aunt Dot sat down and read the list aloud: a baker, a dentist, a man with a boat and three others. She had written a few notes beside each name, including “good teeth” and “loves his mother”.
But the best name, Dot said, was not on the list at all, because he had only just arrived. Dr Ruiz was the new vet, single and kind, and she had booked a table for the two of them that evening.
Wren tried every excuse she had: a deadline, a headache and a cat who needed her. Dot had a cheerful answer to each one, and the answer to the cat was that cats are very independent.
Dot said that if Wren was nervous, she would happily walk her to the restaurant and sit at the next table. Wren had perhaps one second to think of a way out.
Just then the little bell above the café door jingled, and everyone looked up. Wren, who was desperate for an escape, looked up fastest of all.
It was Kit Navarro, the mechanic who kept the little ferry running, with oil on his hands and sleepy eyes. He came in at nine most days for a coffee and never said more than he had to.
Wren knew him only by sight, as the quiet man who hummed over engines on the quay. In two years they had exchanged perhaps ten words, and four of them were about the weather.
Wren stood up so fast that her chair scraped the floor. Pointing at Kit, she announced that she could not go on a date, because she was already seeing someone, and it was him.
Kit froze with one hand on the counter and the other holding a coin in the air. Every head in the café turned towards him, and Mr Pell's mouth fell open.
Kit looked at Wren's frightened face, then at Aunt Dot's hopeful one. Slowly he walked over, put a hand on Wren's shoulder and smiled as if he had been waiting years to be asked.
Aunt Dot clapped her hands and asked how long this had been going on. “A few weeks,” said Kit, without blinking, “but we wanted to keep it quiet.”
Dot took out her phone at once and called the restaurant, then the vet. She cancelled the dinner so cheerfully that Dr Ruiz was probably relieved.
Now they must both come to Sunday lunch at Rose Cottage, Dot said, so that she could look at Kit properly. And in six weeks, at the Lantern Fair, the whole town could meet him too.
Dot swept out of the café, glowing like a lamp, and the room slowly breathed again. Mr Pell winked at them both and said that this morning's coffee was on the house.
Outside, Wren said she was terribly sorry, and she explained that she had panicked. Kit was annoyed, but his mouth kept turning up at the corners, because the whole thing was very funny.
Kit pointed out that Dot had a phone, a notebook and forty friends. By noon, he said, the whole of Salt Cove would know that he was taken.
Kit leaned on the wall, looked out across the bay and admitted something he did not usually say. Since his fiancée Dana had left two years ago, half the town had brought him casseroles and sad looks.
Kit said that, since the lie was already out, they might as well use it. They could pretend until the Lantern Fair and then quietly break up, and nobody would be surprised.
Wren thought of the vet dinner she had escaped and of the six more lists her aunt would write. Saying yes was her great weakness, but for once it seemed to be solving a problem instead of making one.
They slipped back into the café and took the small corner table, where nobody could hear. Mr Pell, who was pretending very badly not to listen, brought them a pen and a fresh paper napkin.

Rule one, Kit wrote in neat capital letters, was NO FEELINGS. Whatever happened in public, he said, nobody was allowed to fall for anybody, and Wren agreed so quickly that he looked slightly offended.
Rule two was different, and Kit said it more quietly. His nephew Leo was eight and lived with him while his mother worked at sea, and nobody was ever to lie to Leo.

Rule three made them both go slightly pink: kisses were allowed only in public, and only when truly needed. Kit wrote it down like a repair instruction, and Wren suddenly found the ceiling very interesting.
Rule four was the simplest: the whole arrangement would end the day after the Lantern Fair. Wren added a tiny dragon in the corner, for luck, and then they both signed their names underneath.

Kit folded the napkin carefully and put it in his shirt pocket, where it would be safe. Then they shook hands, and Wren had a fluttering feeling that she had just signed up for more than a napkin could hold.
That afternoon Wren hurried to the bookshop and told her best friend Marta the whole story. Marta laughed so hard that she had to sit down on a pile of cookery books.
Marta said she sold a hundred books about pretend couples, and every single one ended in love. Wren replied firmly that this was real life, and that real life had rules.
That night Wren lay awake while Pickle, her fat grey cat, snored on the pillow beside her. She had told one small lie in a café, and by tomorrow it would be walking around town in its best coat.
Kit had put his number in her phone, and by Saturday they were swapping facts like spies. She learned that he hated olives and loved storms, and he learned that she ate her toast upside down.

On Sunday they walked up the hill to Rose Cottage with a bunch of flowers from the market. Kit suggested holding hands from the gate, but Wren thought it too soon, so a goat could have walked between them.
The table at Rose Cottage was full: Dot, Marta, Mr Pell and a very large chicken. Dot leaned forward with her fork in the air and asked how the two of them had met, and they had no story at all.
Kit calmly put down his knife and began to tell a story. Wren, he said, had once fallen off the jetty while drawing a seagull, and he had fished her out by the back of her coat.

Wren, trying to help, added that the water had been freezing and that Kit had used a fishing net. Kit gently remarked that it had been a rope, and for a moment they argued about their own invented rescue.
Marta choked on her tea so violently that Mr Pell had to pat her on the back. Dot only smiled a small, knowing smile, as if the muddle were the most charming thing she had ever heard.
While Wren dried the plates, Dot said quietly that Kit was a good man who had been badly hurt. She told Wren to be gentle with him, and Wren felt a prickle of guilt as sharp as a pin.
On Monday morning a short message arrived from Kit, and it was about rule two. Leo had already heard about Wren from three people, and Kit wanted them to meet before anyone invented a story for him.
Kit lived on Anchor Lane, in a small house with a blue door right next to the ferry shed. There was a dragon painted on the doormat, and Wren took a deep breath before she knocked.
Leo opened the door with a toy dragon under his arm and studied Wren from head to toe. Then he asked, in the calm voice of a judge, whether she was Kit's girlfriend.

Wren knelt down and said, truthfully, that she was Kit's friend and would be around quite a lot for a while. Leo thought about this and said that Mr Pell had called her Kit's girlfriend, and Wren admitted that Mr Pell said many things.
Leo led her upstairs to his room, where forty-one dragons stood on a long shelf in order of size. Each one had a name and a history, and he introduced them all with great ceremony.
Leo found out that Wren drew for a living, and he handed her a pencil at once. She drew a round green dragon with a friendly face, and Leo studied it with folded arms and said it looked far too nice.
Wren thought for a moment, then drew sharp teeth and a curl of smoke and gave the dragon a worried frown. Leo said every dragon needs a good reason for its fire, and this one looked as if it had one.
Leo's mother, Rosa, called on the tablet from her research ship, with grey sea and wheeling birds behind her. Kit had already told her the truth, and she laughed until the signal broke up.
Kit cooked fish fingers and peas, which was the only dinner Leo allowed on Mondays. Wren stayed to eat, and she was surprised to find that she was laughing more than she had in weeks.
That night Wren found an email from Ms Halden, an editor at a big publishing house in the city of Barrowfield. She liked Wren's drawings and wanted her to come in for a job interview.
At dawn Wren read the email once more, with Pickle asleep on her knee. Halden and Moss was the very publisher whose books she had loved since she was a girl.
She was excited and frightened at the same time, because a job in Barrowfield would mean leaving Salt Cove. She had never lived anywhere else, and she was not sure she would know how.

Wren told Marta about the email, and Marta squealed so loudly that a customer dropped a book. Marta said Wren must go, and then asked what Kit would think, and Wren said it was a silly question, because it was only pretend.
The next day it rained hard, and Kit was on the quay repairing the ferry. Wren filled a flask with tea and carried it to him, because a girlfriend should, and because half the town was watching.
Kit crawled out from under the engine cover with rain running down his nose. He looked at the flask as if nobody had ever brought him anything before, and then he said a quiet thank you.

Wren asked what was wrong with the engine, and Kit, who usually said very little, explained for ten whole minutes. He talked about fuel pipes, old brass and the way the Gannet had her moods, and for once he forgot to be shy.
By lunchtime everyone in Salt Cove knew that Wren had carried tea to Kit in the pouring rain. Mr Pell had told the story eleven times already, and in his latest version there was a violin.

Kit looked at Wren's face, which was pale with panic, and then at Aunt Dot's, which was bright with hope, and something in his own expression softened. He crossed the floor in four unhurried steps, rested one large hand on Wren's shoulder and gave a slow smile that, to her astonishment, looked entirely convincing. “Good morning, darling,” he said, in the voice of a man who had been waiting years to be asked.

Aunt Dot clapped her hands together so hard that the teaspoons rattled, and demanded to know how long this wonderful secret had been going on. “A few weeks,” said Kit, without so much as a flicker of an eyelid, “but we wanted to keep it quiet until we were sure.” Wren, who had never lied to her aunt in her life, nodded like a toy dog on a dashboard and tried to smile.

Dot, to whom no crisis was ever more than a logistical puzzle, took out her mobile phone and called the restaurant, and then the vet. She cancelled the dinner with such radiant goodwill that poor Dr Ruiz, who had been dreading it all day, thanked her three times and offered to send flowers. Wren watched the whole scene with the dazed gratitude of a person who has jumped out of a window and discovered a haystack.

Now, Dot declared, they must both come to Sunday lunch at Rose Cottage, so that she could examine this young man at close quarters and feed him something nourishing. As for the rest of Salt Cove, it would meet him properly at the Lantern Fair, which was only six weeks away and which Dot chaired with the iron hand of a sea captain. She wrote the date in a small red notebook, and in Wren's mind a door that had been open an inch swung quietly shut.

Dot swept out of the café like a ship leaving harbour under full sail, glowing with triumph, and the room slowly began to breathe again. Mr Pell winked at the two of them with great meaning and announced that this morning's coffee was on the house, which in thirty years he had never done for anyone. Wren understood, with a sinking heart, that by lunchtime half of Salt Cove would know.

Out on the pavement Wren apologised so many times that she lost count, explaining that her aunt had cornered her and that panic had made her point. Kit folded his arms and tried to look cross, but the corners of his mouth kept twitching upward, and at last he gave a short, helpless laugh. It was the first time she had ever heard him laugh, and it was a better sound than she had expected.

Kit explained, with the patience of a man describing the tide to a child, that Dot possessed a telephone, a notebook and at least forty friends. By noon, he said, every baker, fisherman and teacher in Salt Cove would know that he was spoken for, and by supper they would all have an opinion about it. Wren groaned, covered her face with both hands and wished that the pavement would open and take her somewhere with fewer neighbours.

Kit leaned against the harbour wall, looked out across the bay and admitted something he did not usually say aloud. Since his fiancée Dana had left two years ago, the town had treated him like a house with a broken window, bringing casseroles and advice and watching him with a gentle, unbearable pity. He had eaten fourteen lasagnes, he said, and he was heartily sick of every single one of them.

Kit thought for a while, and then he said, slowly, that since the lie was already out in the world they might as well put it to work. They could pretend to be a couple until the Lantern Fair, he suggested, and afterwards let it fade quietly away, as such things do, and nobody would be astonished or sorry. Wren stared at him, and the strangest part, she realised, was that the idea did not sound mad at all.

Wren thought of the dinner she had escaped and of the procession of bakers and dentists that would follow if the truth came out, and her resistance melted like butter on a warm scone. Saying yes was her oldest weakness, but for once it seemed to be solving a problem rather than creating one. She put out her hand, and Kit looked at it for a moment before shaking it gravely.

Kit said that a plan like this needed rules, just as an engine needed a manual, and so they crept back into the café and took the small table in the far corner. Mr Pell, who was pretending very badly not to listen, drifted over with a pen and a fresh paper napkin and then drifted away again, whistling innocently to himself. Kit smoothed the napkin flat with the edge of his hand, uncapped the pen and looked at Wren with the grave expression of a man about to sign a treaty.

Rule one, Kit wrote in neat capital letters, was NO FEELINGS: whatever they performed in public, neither of them was permitted to mean any of it. Wren agreed so quickly and so enthusiastically that he glanced up with a flicker of what might have been offence. It was, she thought, the most sensible rule imaginable, and she could not think why it made her stomach feel odd.

Rule two was different, and Kit said it more quietly, as if it weighed more. His nephew Leo was eight and lived with him while Leo's mother worked on a research ship far away, and nobody, whatever else happened, was to lie to the boy. Kit said he had seen enough promises wear thin, and he would not have the child learn from him how easily it was done.

Rule three made them both go faintly pink, for it stated that there would be no real kissing at all, except in public and only when the performance absolutely required it. Kit wrote it down in the flat, practical tone of a repair instruction, as though a kiss were a washer that might occasionally need replacing. Wren studied the ceiling, which she discovered had never looked so interesting, and counted its cracks with great attention.

Rule four was the simplest of all: the whole arrangement would end, with a polite smile and no hard feelings, on the day after the Lantern Fair. Wren could not resist drawing a small, indignant dragon in the corner of the napkin, as a kind of official seal, and Kit watched her pen move with an expression she could not read. Then they signed their names underneath, like two diplomats agreeing a treaty between very small countries.

Kit folded the napkin in half, then in half again, and slid it into the pocket of his work shirt with the care of a man storing a valuable part. They shook hands on the agreement, and his palm was warm and rough and a good deal larger than she had expected. As he walked away towards the ferry shed, humming under his breath, Wren had the fluttering feeling that she had just signed up for something no napkin could contain.

That afternoon Wren hurried to the bookshop on Harbour Street, where her best friend Marta ran the till, the dust and the opinions, and told her everything. Marta listened without a word, her eyebrows climbing higher with each detail, and then she laughed so helplessly that she had to sit down on a stack of cookery books. When she could speak again, she wiped her eyes and said that Wren had finally found a way to say no to Dot, and that the way involved lying to an entire town.

Marta pointed out, with a gleam in her eye, that she sold a hundred novels about pretend couples every year, and that every single one of them ended in a wedding. Wren replied firmly that this was real life, that Kit was a mechanic and not a hero, and that the whole arrangement came with a napkin of rules. Marta only smiled, pressed a paperback into her hands and called it research, adding that the first chapter was particularly relevant.

That night Wren lay awake in her flat above the sail-maker's shop while Pickle, her enormous grey cat, snored on the pillow beside her like a small, contented engine. She had told one small lie in a café, and by tomorrow it would be strolling about Salt Cove in its best coat, shaking hands with the neighbours. She stared at the ceiling and reminded herself that it was only six weeks, that there were rules, and that nobody in history had ever been seriously hurt by a napkin.

By Saturday they had settled into a nervous rhythm of messages, swapping facts about each other like two spies preparing a cover story. She learned that he hated olives, loved storms and had never once been late for a ferry, while he learned that she was left-handed and cried at the end of every film about a dog. It was a strangely intimate sort of homework, and neither of them mentioned how much they were enjoying it.

On Sunday they climbed the hill to Rose Cottage, a crooked house with a yellow door and a garden that spilled over its fence like a runaway orchestra. Kit carried a bunch of flowers that he had bought with visible embarrassment, and halfway up the path he suggested they hold hands from the gate onwards. Wren said it was far too soon, and so they approached the door with a gap between them that a goat could have walked through.

The table at Rose Cottage was crowded, for Dot had invited Marta as a witness, and Mr Pell had invited himself, and between them sat a roast chicken the size of a small dog. Dot leaned forward with her fork in the air and asked, with an innocence that deceived no one, exactly how the two of them had met. Wren and Kit looked at one another in dawning horror, because in all their careful preparations they had never once planned a story.

Kit calmly put down his knife and began to tell a story, using his hands for emphasis, in the manner of a man describing a particularly large fish. Wren, he said, had been sketching a seagull at the end of the old jetty when the seagull moved and she did not, and he had fished her out by the back of her coat. By the end the whole table was weeping with laughter, and even Mr Pell had stopped chewing.

Wren, determined to help, added that the water had been freezing, that the jetty had been painted green and that Kit had rescued her with a fishing net. Kit remarked mildly that he remembered a rope, and that the jetty had been blue, and for a moment they bickered like an old married couple over a memory that had never existed. Dot watched them with shining eyes, because nothing in the world looks more genuine than two people disagreeing about the past.

Marta choked on her tea so violently that Mr Pell had to pound her on the back, and she retreated behind her napkin with her shoulders shaking. Dot, however, merely smiled a small, thoughtful smile and passed the potatoes, as though she had just been handed an interesting clue. It was only later that Wren wondered how much a woman who had chaired a committee for forty years could really be fooled.

In the kitchen afterwards, while Wren dried the plates, Dot said quietly that Kit was a good man who had been badly hurt, and that it would be kind to be careful with him. Wren agreed, her throat suddenly tight, and felt a prickle of guilt as sharp as a pin, because the person she was fooling was the person who loved her most. Through the window she could see Kit in the garden, crouched beside a dripping tap, mending it without being asked.

On Monday morning a short message arrived from Kit, and it concerned rule two. Leo had already heard about Wren from three different people, including the postman, and Kit wanted them to meet before the town could tell the boy a story of its own. Wren read it twice, finished her tea in one gulp and realised that she was more nervous about meeting an eight-year-old than she had been about lying to a café.

Kit lived at the end of Anchor Lane in a narrow house with a blue door, squeezed beside the ferry shed like a small boat tied up next to a large one. A hand-painted dragon decorated the doormat, a scooter lay abandoned on the step, and from somewhere inside came the sound of a very determined eight-year-old singing about pirates. Wren took a deep breath, straightened her cardigan and knocked twice, with all the confidence of someone visiting a dentist.

Leo, small and serious and clutching a green toy dragon, opened the door before Kit could reach it and examined Wren from head to toe with the thoroughness of a customs officer. Behind him Kit hovered in the hallway with the look of a man who has left his tools somewhere inconvenient. Then Leo asked, in a voice of perfect innocence, whether she was Kit's girlfriend.

Wren knelt down to his level and said, with careful honesty, that she was Kit's friend and that she would be around quite a lot for the next few weeks. Leo considered this answer from every angle, and then he remarked that Mr Pell had told him she was Kit's girlfriend, and that Mr Pell was usually right about gossip. Wren admitted that Mr Pell had a great deal to say and that not all of it could be trusted, and Kit coughed into his hand to hide a smile.

Leo led her up a steep little staircase to his bedroom, where forty-one dragons stood to attention along a long shelf, arranged strictly in order of size. Each one had a name, a favourite food and a complicated history, and he introduced the whole company with the solemnity of a king presenting his army. Soot, he explained, was the grumpy one, Ember was the brave one, and a small purple dragon called Pudding was afraid of thunder but would never admit it.

When Leo discovered that Wren drew pictures for a living, he handed her a pencil and a sheet of paper with the air of a man commissioning a portrait. She drew a round green dragon with a friendly face and a curly tail, and Leo studied it for a long time with his arms folded, like a critic in a gallery. It was good, he said at last, but it looked far too nice, and a proper dragon needed to look as if it might eat a small castle.

Wren thought for a moment, rubbed out the smile and gave the dragon sharp teeth, a curl of smoke and a deeply worried frown. Leo leaned in close and approved, announcing that a dragon only breathes fire for a reason, and that this one was clearly guarding something important. They shook hands on it, and Wren wondered whether she had ever been paid a better compliment.

At six o'clock Leo's mother, Rosa, called on the tablet from her research ship, with a grey sea and a cloud of wheeling birds behind her. Kit had told her the whole truth the night before, and she greeted Wren with such warm and wicked amusement that Wren felt, absurdly, that she had been adopted. Behind her brother's back she mouthed the words “good luck”, and then the signal crackled and she was gone.

Kit cooked fish fingers and peas, which by long tradition was the only dinner that Leo permitted on a Monday, and Wren was invited to stay and help eat them. Leo talked without pausing about dragons, football and a boy at school who could burp the alphabet, while Kit said very little and listened to every word with obvious love. Somewhere between the second pea and the third, Wren realised that she was laughing more than she had in weeks.

That night an email arrived from a Ms Halden, an editor at the large publishing house of Halden and Moss in the faraway city of Barrowfield. She had seen Wren's work, she wrote, and she admired it enormously, and she wondered whether Wren might come in for an interview about a full-time position. Wren read it three times and then closed the laptop very quietly, as though it might bite.

At dawn she read the email a fourth time, with Pickle asleep on her knee and a cold cup of tea forgotten beside the bed. Halden and Moss was the publisher whose books had lined her shelves since childhood, the one she had secretly imagined while drawing animals at the kitchen table at the age of nine. It seemed impossible that anyone in that glossy, distant world had noticed a woman sketching foxes in a café by the sea.

She felt two things at once, like a person on a swing: a bright, fizzing excitement, and a heavy fear that sat in her stomach like a stone. A job in Barrowfield would mean leaving Salt Cove, its gulls and its harbour, her aunt and her best friend and even, she noticed with surprise, a certain quiet mechanic whom she had known for barely a week. She told herself firmly that she would not think about any of it until she had to, which was her favourite way of solving every problem.

Wren told Marta about the email, and Marta squealed so loudly that a customer in the poetry section dropped a book on his foot. She declared that Wren must go to the interview, must wear the green dress, and must on no account say yes to the first thing anyone offered her. Then she asked, with studied casualness, what Kit would think, and Wren said it was a ridiculous question, because Kit was only pretend.

The next morning the rain came down in grey ropes, and Kit was out on the quay with his head inside the Gannet's engine cover, repairing something stubborn. Wren filled a flask with strong sweet tea and carried it along the wet jetty in her yellow raincoat, because a girlfriend ought to, and because half of Salt Cove was watching from behind its curtains. She told herself that it was purely a performance, though she noticed that she had put in an extra spoonful of sugar.

Kit emerged from under the engine cover with rain running down his nose and a spanner clutched in one fist, and he looked at the flask as though it were a rare and unexpected animal. It had been a long time since anyone had thought to bring him anything, he said gruffly, and for a moment he simply held the steaming cup in both hands without drinking. Then he thanked her, very quietly, and the rain itself seemed to soften, as if even the weather had been listening.

Wren asked what was wrong with the engine, and Kit, who normally rationed his words like wartime sugar, explained for ten whole minutes without stopping. He spoke of fuel pipes and salt corrosion and the stubborn old brass that had served three generations of ferry captains, and he spoke of the Gannet as if she were a clever, temperamental aunt. Wren, who understood perhaps one word in five, listened with her chin on her hand and found that she did not mind at all.

By lunchtime everyone in Salt Cove knew that Wren had carried a flask of tea to Kit in the pouring rain, because Mr Pell had told the story to eleven customers and a visiting postman. With each telling the details had grown more romantic, until the tea had become a hot dinner, the raincoat had become a velvet cloak and there was, somewhere in the background, a violin. Wren listened to the final version from the doorway and decided that she would never again underestimate the creative power of a small town.

That afternoon Aunt Dot telephoned, so delighted that Wren had to hold the receiver at arm's length like a small, noisy animal. She had heard about the tea, she had heard about the raincoat, and she wished to know whether Kit had said anything romantic in return. Wren replied that he had said thank you, and Dot sighed with deep satisfaction and said that this was exactly how the best love stories began.

That evening Kit sent a message, which was short, as all his messages were, thanking her for the tea and complimenting the excellence of her performance. He added that the town would expect to see them together at the Saturday market, and that they should practise, as they could not yet walk side by side without a goat's width between them. Wren read it three times, decided that three was the sensible limit, and then read it a fourth.

That night Wren settled down to the last pictures of The Sleepy Lighthouse, with a lamp, a pot of tea and Pickle stretched across the paper like a furry paperweight. When she looked down an hour later, she discovered that Percy had acquired a neighbour: a little ferry in the margin, with a small, bent figure working on its engine. She rubbed it out, and then, with a sigh she did not quite understand, she drew it in again.

On Saturday the quay was crowded with stalls under striped awnings, selling everything from smoked fish and sourdough to handmade soap and secondhand books, while the air smelled of salt, bread and frying onions. Wren found Kit waiting beside the fruit stall in a clean shirt, looking as nervous as a man about to have a tooth out. Every single person at the market, she realised, was pretending very hard not to look at them.

They took each other's hand with the grim determination of two people defusing a bomb. Kit gripped her fingers as though she were a delicate part that might snap, while Wren held her own hand so stiffly that it might have been carved from wood. They shuffled past three stalls in painful silence, and neither of them could remember ever having had so many knuckles.

Mrs Abara, who had sold cheese for twenty years and held decided views on romance, called out that they looked like two people carrying a wardrobe up a narrow staircase. Everyone within earshot laughed, kindly but without the smallest attempt to hide it, and Wren's cheeks turned the colour of the tomatoes on the next stall. Kit, to her surprise, laughed too, a low and genuine laugh, and for a moment his hand in hers relaxed.

Marta, who was running the bookshop's stall at the end of the row, hurried over with the brisk authority of a theatre director. She told them to drop their shoulders, match their steps and stop thinking about their hands, because a hand that is being thought about always looks like a hand that is lying. Then she pushed them gently back into the crowd and returned to her books, looking enormously pleased with herself.

They tried again, walking slowly and in step, while Kit told her in a low voice about the market's oldest fishmonger, who had once sold a haddock to a famous actor. Somewhere between the fish and the flowers, their hands stopped being a problem and simply became hands, warm and loosely linked, swinging a little between them. It was entirely natural, Wren thought with some alarm, and it was only supposed to be a performance.

Mr Pell, who had taken a bun stall at the market purely, it seemed, to supervise them, called out in a carrying voice that a couple so happy ought to prove it. Half the quay turned to look, and Kit, after one brief glance at Wren that asked a silent question, bent his head and kissed her cheek, so lightly that she might have imagined it. Mr Pell led the applause, a dozen strangers joined in, and Wren felt the whole world tilt a few degrees to the left.

Wren's cheek tingled as if it had been touched by a spark, and Kit stared at a cabbage on the nearest stall with the fierce concentration of a man reading a very difficult map. Neither of them spoke for a full minute, which was entirely ordinary for Kit and deeply alarming for Wren, who usually filled any silence with chatter. Rule three, she reminded herself sternly, had been followed to the letter, and there was no reason whatsoever for her heart to be behaving like this.

At the flower stall Kit bought her a small bunch of sweet peas, pink and white and smelling of summer, before he seemed to have decided to do it. Then he went red to the tips of his ears and explained, in a rush, that it was merely a good idea for the act, since people would notice if he never gave her anything. Wren thanked him gravely, buried her nose in the flowers to hide her smile and did not tell him that nobody had bought her flowers in three years.

Before they left, one leg of Mrs Abara's cheese stall began to wobble alarmingly, and Kit was on his knees under it at once, tightening a bolt with a coin from his pocket. Wren noticed that he was humming softly while he worked, a wandering tune with no name, and that his whole face had changed, as though all his cares had been set down on the cobbles beside him. She had never seen anyone look so entirely at peace, and she stood there much longer than a pretend girlfriend needed to.

That night Wren sat at her kitchen table with her pencils and drew Kit from memory, kneeling beneath the stall with his head tilted and a coin held between his fingers. She could not leave out the hum, and so she added it, in tiny curling lines of pencil that drifted up from his mouth like smoke from a chimney. It was the best drawing she had made in a year, and she tucked it between two pages of her sketchbook as though she were hiding evidence.

On Sunday morning Leo burst into Pell's Café with Kit trailing behind him, demanding at the top of his voice to know whether his dragon was finished. Wren, who had promised him a second drawing, dug her sketchbook out of her bag in a hurry, and in her haste a loose page slid out and fluttered onto the table. It landed face up between the teacups, exactly where a certain mechanic could see it.

Kit picked up the page before Wren could snatch it away, and for a long time he looked at it in silence, at the tilt of his own head and the little curls of hum drifting from his mouth. Nobody had ever drawn him before, he said at last, in a voice rougher than usual, and he had not known that he could look so content. Then he held it as carefully as if it were made of glass and asked, quite seriously, whether he might keep it.

While Leo drew a fire-breathing dragon on a paper placemat, Kit said quietly that he had never noticed his own humming until that moment. Dana used to say it drove her mad, he admitted, and he had spent years trying to stop, because a habit that annoys the person you love is not one you can keep. Wren told him, with more heat than she had intended, that it was the nicest sound in the whole of Salt Cove.

Wren tore the page carefully from the sketchbook and handed it over, feeling absurdly shy about it. Kit folded the drawing in half and slid it into his shirt pocket, right next to the napkin with the rules, and patted the pocket once as if to make sure that both were safe. Leo, without looking up from his dragon, remarked that this was where Kit kept the things that mattered, and Kit pretended not to hear.

On Monday Marta stood among her shelves with her arms folded and the stern expression of a headmistress, and informed Wren that she was a terrible actress. She had watched her at the market, she said, and nobody had ever faked that look, which belonged to a woman who had been kissed on the cheek and was still thinking about it. Wren protested that the look was a trick of the light, and Marta raised one eyebrow so high that it nearly vanished into her hair.

Marta offered a wager: if the pretending turned real before the Lantern Fair, Wren would buy her a cinnamon bun every Friday for a year, and if it did not, Marta would do the same. Wren shook her hand at once, with the serene confidence of a woman who is absolutely sure of her own heart. She walked home in the afternoon light, entirely certain that she would win, and quietly puzzled by a small, treacherous doubt about which result she was hoping for.

On a still, golden evening, after the last crossing of the day, Kit took the Gannet out into the bay and let Wren take the wheel. He stood just behind her, explaining in his quiet voice how to turn gently against the current, and she could feel the warmth of him through the thin cloth of her shirt. She was happy, she realised, and that, she knew very well, was precisely the problem.

Kit taught her to read the bay as one reads a page: the dark patches where the water ran deep, the pale ripples that warned of rocks, the long smooth slick where the tide was turning. Wren, who had spent years drawing the sea, understood that she had never truly looked at it until now. It was a strange and humbling pleasure to be taught by a man who had studied the water all his life and had never once tried to draw it.

Out on the water there was no audience at all, not so much as a curious gull, and yet neither of them moved away from the other. They talked about everything and nothing, about Leo's dragons and Wren's lighthouse, about the engine's moods and the sea's, and it was a very long time before either remembered that they were supposed to be pretending. When Wren finally did, the realisation felt like stepping on a stair that was not there.

After they had tied up the ferry for the night, they sat on the harbour wall beneath a sky crowded with stars, intending to stay for a single minute. The minute stretched into an hour and then into two, softened by the sound of the water slapping against the stones, and Wren could not have said where the time had gone. They were supposed to have said goodnight long before, according to the unspoken logic of their arrangement, and neither of them had mentioned it.

Kit told her that his father had kept the Gannet running for thirty years, and that he had grown up in her engine room, perched on an upturned bucket, learning every bolt by name. His father was a patient man who spoke through his hands, he said, and Kit had inherited the habit along with the spanners and the stubbornness. His father had retired to a bungalow on the south coast, he added, and sent postcards of other people's ferries.

Wren told him about the summers of her childhood, when her parents had moved from city to city for their work and she had been sent to Rose Cottage with a suitcase and a box of crayons. Aunt Dot had given her a pencil, a kitchen table and unlimited paper, and over the years Salt Cove had quietly become the only place where she had ever felt entirely at home. That was why she had never imagined leaving, she said carefully, and she did not mention the email that was sitting, unanswered, in her phone.

Kit threw a pebble into the dark water and watched the rings spread, and then he said, almost to himself, that people leave, and that it is easier not to ask them to stay. Wren answered that her own trouble was the opposite, since she could not say no to anyone, and that she had once spent a whole summer running a jam stall because a stranger had looked disappointed. They sat for a while with these two small confessions between them, like two shells set side by side on a wall.

Across the sleeping rooftops the church clock began to strike, and they both counted the chimes under their breath without meaning to. When it reached twelve, they turned to each other in astonishment, as though the town had played a trick on them and stolen two hours. It was the first time in years, Kit admitted, that he had stayed up past ten for any reason other than a broken engine.

Kit draped his jacket around her shoulders, because the night air had turned cold, and walked her home through the empty lanes, with the streetlamps making small gold islands on the pavement. Halfway along Gull Lane Wren noticed that their hands were linked, and that they had been linked for some time, and that there was not a single person in the street to see it. Neither of them said a word, but they let go, rather quickly, at her door, like two people caught doing something forbidden.

In the morning Wren woke to find Pickle sitting on her chest like a small, disapproving judge, and Kit's jacket hanging from the back of her chair. She told herself sternly that rule one still applied, that a jacket was only a jacket and that her heart, whatever it thought it was doing, had not been consulted. Then she hid her face in her hands, because the jacket smelled of salt, engine oil and something warm she could not name, and she was too honest to pretend she had not noticed.

On Wednesday Dot called a meeting of the Lantern Fair committee in the town hall, and she gave out the jobs like a general distributing medals. Wren, who had of course agreed to everything, was to paint a hundred paper lanterns and design the posters, while Kit was to mend the old wooden frames and test the floating rafts. They would work at the same long table, Dot added sweetly, because young love ought to be seen.

On Thursday evening Kit sent a message that was much longer than usual, and Wren could almost see him deleting and rewriting it on the other side of town. His old fiancée, Dana, was coming back to Salt Cove for the weekend, he wrote, because her cousin Felix was getting married in the chapel on Saturday, and the whole town would be there to watch. At the bottom, after a long gap, he had added a last line asking whether she would still be willing to play her part.

Wren phoned him at once, ignoring the unwritten rule that they only spoke by message, and told him that of course she would be there. After a long silence, Kit admitted, in a voice she had never heard him use, that he had not seen Dana in two years and could not guess what he would feel. Wren said she would stand beside him the entire time, and she discovered, with some surprise, that she meant every word of it.

On Friday morning Kit and Wren were sharing a table in Pell's Café, arguing amiably over the last cinnamon bun, when the door opened and let in a gust of cold air. A tall woman in a beautifully cut coat stood on the threshold with a suitcase at her feet and sleek dark hair blowing across her face. She was looking straight at Kit, and Wren, who had never met her, knew at once exactly who she was.

Mr Pell dropped a teaspoon with a clang that rang through the silent café like a dinner bell at a funeral. Everybody there remembered Dana, who had once stood in this very doorway holding Kit's arm and a bridal magazine, and nobody had forgotten the winter morning when she left on the early ferry with two suitcases. Dozens of small, curious glances flew between the tables like swallows, and every one of them landed on Kit.

Kit rose from his chair so slowly that it seemed to Wren he was lifting something enormously heavy, and his face went carefully blank, the way a harbour looks before a storm.
