Dana said his name very softly, with a catch in her voice, as though she was not at all certain she still had the right to say it. For a few endless seconds neither of them moved, and Wren found that she was holding her teacup so tightly that it was a wonder it had not cracked.

Then Kit seemed to remember where he was, and who was with him, and he reached out and drew Wren gently to his side with an arm around her waist. His voice was perfectly steady when he introduced her as Wren, his girlfriend, and only Wren, who was pressed against his ribs, could feel how fast his heart was going. It was a flawless performance, and the strangest thing was that Wren could no longer tell whether her own racing heart was acting as well.

For one second Dana's eyes widened, and something that looked very much like sadness crossed her face, as quickly as a cloud crosses a field. Then she smiled, a graceful, generous smile, and took Wren's hand in both of her own, saying that she was very glad to meet her. Kit deserved to be happy, she added, so softly that only Wren could hear, and she sounded as though she meant it with all her heart.

That afternoon Dana was waiting at the school gate with a present for Leo, a small glass dragon wrapped in tissue paper, and she crouched down to give it to him, smiling hopefully. Leo took it and thanked her with perfect politeness, which for a boy who usually shouted his opinions was a very bad sign. He remembered her, Wren realised, and he remembered the morning she left, and he had not yet decided what to do about either.

Dana invited them both to her cousin's wedding in the chapel on Saturday, and to the party that would follow in the Anchor Hall, where half of Salt Cove would be eating cake and having opinions. Kit hesitated, torn between politeness and a strong desire to be elsewhere, and it was Wren, who had never refused an invitation in her life, who said yes for both of them. She regretted it almost at once, and then she saw the look of quiet relief on Dana's face, and regretted it a little less.

Later that afternoon Dana found Wren alone in the bookshop, where Marta had tactfully slipped out to fetch tea, and stood beside her at the window as though they were two strangers waiting for a bus. She said in a low, careful voice that she hoped Wren would not mind a little advice from the one person in town who had no right to give it. Kit felt everything more deeply than anyone she had ever met, she said, and he had never once been able to say so.

Two years earlier, Dana said, she had been offered a post in a city far to the north, and she had shown Kit the letter on the very day it arrived. She waited an entire year for him to ask her to stay, hoping at every breakfast and every farewell that he would utter one small sentence, but he never said a word, so in the end she went. It had been the hardest decision of her life and the only one she could have made, she told Wren, and she still could not decide who was more to blame.

Wren began to defend him, hotly and at some length, and Dana listened with a kind and weary smile, as though she had heard those very arguments from her own mouth a hundred times. He cared more than anyone she had ever known, she said, but the words simply would not come, and if Wren wanted something from him she must say so plainly and not wait to be asked. Then she touched Wren's arm lightly, said that she was glad Kit had someone, and left the shop before Wren could discover that she had no reply at all.

Wren walked alone along the shore at low tide, with her shoes dangling from one hand and the wet sand cold beneath her feet. None of this was real, she told herself, and Dana had been talking about a man who did not belong to her at all, so it made no sense whatsoever that her heart should ache like a bruise. Out on the grey water the Gannet was crossing to Marram, small and steady, and she watched it until her eyes stung.

That evening, while Leo was upstairs arranging his dragons for the night, Wren knocked at the blue door and was let into the kitchen, where a single lamp lit the table. She had rehearsed a gentle, sensible way of beginning on the whole walk up Anchor Lane, and when she opened her mouth she asked him instead, bluntly, why he never talked about his feelings. The words dropped into the quiet kitchen like stones into a deep, dark well, and nothing came back up.

Kit went very still, and slowly folded his arms across his chest, like a man closing the shutters on a house. Feelings, he said in a flat, polite voice, were covered by rule one, and since rule one stated that there would be none, this was not a conversation they needed to have. Wren could hear the clock ticking on the wall and the tap dripping into the sink, and for the first time in her life she did not feel like saying yes.

Wren said, as gently as she could, that Dana had told her about the year she had waited for him to ask her to stay. Kit turned his face to the dark window, and a muscle moved in his jaw, and he said in a low and level voice that Dana had no right to discuss him with anyone. It was not anger that she heard beneath the words, though, but something much older and more bruised, and it made her want to cross the room and hold him.

They argued for a minute, fast and fierce and in whispers, the way people do when a child is upstairs. Wren said that it was not fair to hide behind a napkin, and Kit said that the napkin was the only thing that had made any of this possible. Then they both said sorry at the same moment, and the silence that followed was heavier than the argument had been.

Suddenly there was a tremendous crash in the yard, followed by a long and wounded wail, and Kit was through the back door before Wren had even finished turning round. She ran after him and found Leo sitting on the wet flagstones beside his bicycle, which lay on its side with one wheel bent into the shape of a pretzel. He had sneaked out to practise a jump, he sobbed, and the jump had not gone as planned.

Kit knelt on the wet stones and examined Leo's grazed knee with the care of a surgeon, then lifted the boy's chin and wiped his face with the heel of his hand. The words that Wren had been told he did not possess poured out of him, low and steady and endlessly kind, assuring Leo that he was brave, loved and worth far more than any bicycle. She stood in the doorway without breathing, because it had just occurred to her that Kit had plenty of words for the people he was sure would stay.

On Saturday morning the three of them gathered in Kit's garage, among tins of oil and coils of rope and the smell of warm metal, to mend the bicycle. Kit straightened the wheel with a patient, practised hand, Wren held the frame steady, and Leo, with a bandaged knee and a new sense of importance, was appointed Chief of Spanners. Nobody mentioned the argument of the night before, which hovered over them politely like a guest who has not been introduced.

They worked so smoothly together that nobody needed to ask for anything: Wren held, Kit tightened, Leo passed the right spanner at the right moment. At one point Kit's hand closed over hers on the handlebar to steady it, and neither of them pulled away until the bolt was tight. For a few quiet minutes the three of them were exactly like a family, and nobody dared say so aloud in case the feeling broke.

Leo looked up from the wheel and asked, in the casual tone children use for the questions that matter most, whether she was going to go away like Dana did. Wren, who had promised herself that she would never lie to him, said that she lived in Salt Cove and always had, and that nobody could be sure what next year would bring. Kit, bent over the bolt, did not look up, but his hands stopped moving for a long moment.

At last the bicycle was mended, and Leo wobbled up and down Anchor Lane on it, shouting that it was better than new and that nothing in the world could stop him now. Wren and Kit stood side by side at the gate and watched, a careful hand's breadth apart, saying nothing. Out over the bay great purple clouds were building, the gulls had fallen silent and the wind had begun to smell of rain, so that even the washing on the lines seemed to hold its breath.

Before the wedding Marta came to Wren's flat with a hairbrush, a handful of pins and strong opinions, and helped her into the best blue dress that she owned. When she had finished, she stepped back and studied her friend for a long moment with her head on one side, like an artist assessing a finished canvas. Kit Navarro, she announced at last, was in serious trouble, and it was a pity that he had not been warned.

Kit was waiting at the bottom of the stairs in a dark suit that was a little too tight across the shoulders, holding his hat like a man at a funeral. When he saw Wren, he opened his mouth, closed it again and stood there with all the words he could not find written plainly across his face. In the end he held out a paper bag containing a warm cinnamon bun, and Wren, who spoke fluent Kit by now, understood it perfectly as a compliment.

The small stone chapel was packed to its walls with half of Salt Cove, and white flowers hung from the end of every pew like small waterfalls. Felix and his bride, Hazel, promised to love each other for the rest of their lives in voices that shook with happiness, and the sound of sniffing rose from the congregation like a gentle tide. Wren, sitting beside Kit with her hand in his, was horrified to discover that she was crying too.

On the chapel steps Mr Pell produced an old brass-trimmed camera from his coat and insisted on taking a photograph of the happy couple. Confetti rained down on them in a bright blizzard, settling on Wren's hair and Kit's shoulders, and for once Kit did not look like a man waiting for a bus that would never come. When the shutter clicked, Wren was laughing, he was smiling at her, and neither of them was doing a single thing for the audience.

The party in the Anchor Hall was loud and golden and warm, with a fiddle band in one corner, strings of lanterns across the beams and a wedding cake nearly as tall as a child. The whole of Salt Cove seemed to be present, eating, shouting over the music and watching the couple who had arrived together with the unconcealed interest of a town that has nothing better to do. Wren felt like a goldfish in a particularly well-lit bowl, and she smiled until her cheeks ached.

Across the crowded hall Dana raised her glass to Kit with a small, rueful smile, and something went through his face like a wave through water, part regret, part gratitude and part pure bewilderment. Wren saw it, and she remembered her promise on the phone, and without a moment's thought she slipped her hand into his and held it hard. He looked down at her in surprise, and then, very slowly, he held on.

The fiddlers slid into a slow waltz, and Mr Pell, who had a great gift for making things awkward, announced at the top of his voice that the happy couple would lead the dance. A circle cleared in the middle of the floor with the speed of a crowd that senses a good story, and Kit looked at the boards while Wren looked at the beams. Neither of them could find a single excuse that the entire town would accept.

Kit trod on her foot twice and apologised twice, and then, quite suddenly, he stopped counting the steps and simply moved, as a man moves who has finally decided to trust the water. Under the lanterns the crowd seemed to dissolve, until nothing was left in the world but the warmth of his hand at her back, the sigh of the fiddles and the slow, dizzying turn of the floor. Wren looked up, and he was already looking down, and neither of them was acting.

When the last note faded, the crowd erupted in applause, and Kit let go of her hand a full second too late, which she noticed and chose not to mention. At that very moment a peal of thunder rattled the windows, the great doors banged open and a gust of wet wind blew out half the candles on the tables. The storm that had been brewing all day over the bay had arrived, and it had not come to be polite.

Kit and Wren ran through the streaming streets to Rose Cottage, holding their coats over their heads and laughing helplessly, to fetch Leo from Aunt Dot's. Dot wrapped the sleepy boy in three blankets and a scarf, refused all offers of an umbrella for herself and waved them off with the grim cheer of a woman who had weathered worse. As they struggled down the hill towards Anchor Lane, the streetlamps went out one by one in front of them, until all of Salt Cove lay dark beneath the roaring sky.

Soaked to the skin, they reached the blue door at last, and Leo woke up in Kit's arms and looked about him at the dark hall with enormous, shining eyes. Far from being frightened, he announced that a power cut was the best thing that had ever happened to him and that he intended to stay awake for all of it. Wren found a pile of towels in the hall cupboard and lit the first candle with fingers that would not stop shaking, from cold or from something else.

The whole street was dark, and the electric stove was as much use as a painting of a stove, so Kit dug out an old camping stove from the garage and set a dozen candles along the kitchen table. Wren, who had never in her life been able to leave a hungry person alone, raided the cupboards and found tomatoes, lentils, an onion and half a stale loaf. Between them they began to make soup, in a kitchen that flickered gold and shadow like the cabin of a ship.

They cooked in the flickering light, colliding gently at every turn, as two people do in a small kitchen when neither has the faintest idea what the other will do next. Kit wept freely over the onions and blamed the smoke, and Wren laughed so hard that she dropped the wooden spoon into the pot and had to fish it out with a fork. It was the happiest she had been in weeks, and she saw no reason to examine why.

Three bowls of soup steamed on the kitchen table, and the candles turned the room into a warm brown cave while the storm threw handfuls of rain at the windows. Leo told them a long and winding tale of a dragon who was terrified of thunder, and everyone at the table understood that it was really about Pudding, and that it was also, a little, about Leo. When the thunder crashed outside, Wren and Kit exchanged a look over the boy's head that said, quite plainly, that nobody was going to mention it.

Halfway through a long sentence about the dragon's second adventure, Leo yawned enormously, curled up on the sofa and fell asleep with Pudding tucked under his chin. Kit covered him with a blanket and stood looking down at him for a moment, with an expression so tender and so unguarded that Wren had to look away. The house grew quiet, and the storm outside seemed to wrap them in a small private world.

Kit sat with both hands wrapped around a mug of tea and told her, without being asked, about the morning that Dana left. He had stood on the quay, he said, watching the Gannet, which he had mended for ten years, carry her away, while every word he wanted to say stuck in his throat like a fish bone. He had watched until the ferry was a dot, and then he had gone to work, because the engine did not care what had happened to him.

Wren reached across the table and laid her hand over his, with no audience and no excuse. She asked him, very quietly, what he would have said if the words had come, and the question hung in the candlelight between them like a small flame. Kit looked at her for so long that she thought he would not answer, and then he said, in a voice that barely carried, that he would have said stay.

A smudge of tomato soup had found its way onto her cheek, and Kit, without appearing to decide to do it, reached out and wiped it away with his thumb. His hand stayed where it was, warm and rough against her skin, and the whole world narrowed to the width of a candle flame. Somewhere far away the wind was howling and the shutters were rattling, but in that kitchen there was no sound at all.

Kit rose slowly from his chair, and so did Wren, and somehow the table was no longer between them and they were standing very close in the shifting gold light. His eyes went to her mouth and then back to her eyes, asking a question that neither of them had ever dared to put into words. She felt herself leaning towards him as a plant leans towards a window, and she could not have said which of them moved first.

At the last possible moment Wren heard herself whisper the single word rules, and the spell shattered like glass. Kit stepped back at once, his face unreadable in the candlelight, and gave a short, stiff nod that was somehow worse than any argument. She walked home through the thinning rain under his big black umbrella, and when she looked back from her own door, he was still standing in his, holding a single candle.

On Sunday morning the whole town trooped down to the beach to inspect the damage, in wellington boots and in the unmistakable mood of people who have survived something together. The storm had torn up a fence, flooded the chapel steps, sunk two rowing boats and heaped a long, silvery mountain of driftwood along the tideline, as if the sea had been spring-cleaning. Wren stood at the edge of it with her hands in her pockets and did not look for Kit, which took a surprising amount of effort.

At noon Dana left on the Gannet, and Wren watched from the far end of the quay as she said goodbye to Kit, close enough to see their faces and too far to hear a word. Kit spoke for a long time, for Kit, with his hands moving awkwardly at his sides, and Dana listened with her head bowed. When he had finished, she kissed his cheek, and her face crumpled and then cleared, like a sky after rain.

Kit walked slowly along the quay and stopped beside her, with his hands in his pockets and the look of a man who has put down something heavy and has not yet learned to stand without it. He had told Dana he was sorry that he had never asked her to stay, he said, and she had told him that it was two years late and that she forgave him all the same. Then he looked out at the empty bay and added, with the ghost of a smile, that it was easier to say than he had expected, but only to somebody who was already leaving.

On Monday Wren went into the bookshop, turned the sign on the door to closed, and told Marta in a small, flat voice that her feelings for Kit had stopped being pretend. Marta, who had been waiting for this moment with the patience of a cat at a mousehole, did not say I told you so, which Wren recognised as the greatest act of friendship she had ever witnessed. She simply came round the counter and hugged her, hard, and said that bun debts could wait.

Marta said that she must tell him the truth at once, before the Lantern Fair arrived and the napkin expired. Wren answered that rule one was written in Kit's own handwriting and kept in his own pocket, and that she would rather be his pretend girlfriend for another three weeks than risk being nothing to him at all. It was the first time in her life, she realised, that keeping quiet felt like cowardice instead of kindness.

Over the next few evenings Kit and Leo hauled the very best planks of driftwood up the beach to the ferry shed, choosing only the ones that were silver-grey and smooth and shaped by years of salt. Leo had been sworn to secrecy about the project, with a handshake and a solemn promise, and he kept his word for very nearly an hour. By the second evening the whole of Pell's Café knew that Kit Navarro was building something in his shed, and that it was a surprise.

Late at night, in the quiet of the ferry shed, Kit sanded a small desk with long, patient strokes, humming under his breath. He had measured it for a left-handed artist, shaped one edge to rest her elbow and cut a groove for her pencils. It was the first thing he had made in years that was not meant to float, and he was making it, he told himself, not for the pretend girlfriend but for the real woman.

On Wednesday another email arrived from Ms Halden, offering a time for the interview: ten o'clock in the morning on the Friday eight days before the Lantern Fair. Wren read it standing up, as though sitting down would make it too real, and then she printed it, folded it small and hid it in a cookery book, where she kept everything she was not ready to face. She had not told Kit, and the longer she waited, the heavier the secret grew, until it felt like a stone in her coat pocket.

By Thursday the desk was finished, and Kit carried it up the creaking stairs to the empty loft above the ferry shed, where a great window opened on the whole wide silver stretch of the bay. He set it beneath the glass, stepped back to judge the light and decided with a faint, secret smile that the sea had never looked better. Then he covered it with an old sail and told Leo, for the fifth time, that it must be a surprise until he found the right moment, whatever that was.

That night Wren stood at her window and watched a single light burning in the ferry shed across the dark harbour, steady as a small star. She told Pickle that she would tell Kit everything tomorrow, the email, the interview and the fear, and Pickle, who had heard such promises before, yawned and went back to sleep. It was a good plan, she thought, and then she remembered how many good plans she had kept in cookery books.

On Friday morning Leo ran up to Wren on the quay, waving a crumpled note from his teacher and shouting before he had even stopped. His school was holding Dragon Day, with stories, costumes and a visiting guest, and Leo had told his entire class, quite without consulting anyone, that a real artist would come and teach them to draw dragons. Wren, who had never refused a child, an aunt or a stranger with a clipboard, discovered that she was already saying yes.

Salt Cove School was hung from floor to ceiling with paper dragons, green and gold and purple, and Mrs Tully, Leo's teacher, a brisk and cheerful woman with chalk on her sleeve, shook Wren's hand with tremendous warmth. She confessed that the whole staff room had been following the story of Wren and Kit for a fortnight, like a serial in a magazine, and that the general view was extremely favourable. Wren smiled until her face hurt and tried not to think about the lie growing larger with every kind word.

Thirty children sat cross-legged on the rug and stared at Wren as though she were a rare and possibly dangerous animal, and her mouth went dry. Then Leo stood up, announced in a ringing voice that she was his friend and the best artist in the whole world, and ordered everyone to be quiet or else. The silence that followed was so complete that Wren could hear the clock, and her nerves, to her surprise, melted away.

Wren drew a huge dragon on the whiteboard in sweeping strokes of blue marker, while the children shouted out what it needed: wings, spikes, scales, a tail as long as a train. She gave it all of them, and then, with a flourish, a tiny pair of reading glasses perched on the end of its nose, which made the whole class shriek with joy. By the time the dragon was finished, she had forgotten to be anxious about anything at all.

Wren told them the most important rule she knew about dragons, which she had learned from a boy in the front row: that every dragon needs a reason for its fire. The children took to the idea with ferocious creativity, and within ten minutes the room was full of drawings of dragons that breathed flames to toast marshmallows, to guard a birthday cake or to keep a lost baby penguin warm. Leo watched from the front with his arms folded and a look of such deep, quiet pride that Wren had to blink hard.

At the back of the hall, half hidden behind a stack of small chairs, Kit stood with his arms folded and the look of a man who is watching something wonderful and does not wish to be noticed. When Wren caught his eye, he did not look away, as he usually did, but held her gaze with a warmth so open that she lost her place in the middle of a sentence. Somewhere in the back of her mind a small voice pointed out that nobody had asked him to look at her like that, and that there was no rule for it.

After school they sat on a bench by the harbour, with Leo racing his bicycle up and down the quay in full view, and Wren finally told Kit everything. A publisher in Barrowfield had invited her to interview for a full-time job, she said, the kind most illustrators dream about, and she had known for almost two weeks and been too frightened to tell him. She watched his face the entire time, and it did not change at all.

Kit said at once that he was happy for her, that it was wonderful news and that of course she must go, because nobody with her talent should waste it on a seaside café. His voice was kind and steady and perfectly even, but his hands were gripping his knees so tightly that his knuckles had gone white, and he did not look at her once. It was a very good performance, Wren thought, and it was the first time she had ever hated one.

Wren waited for him to say stay, or to say anything at all that was not polite, and the silence between them stretched as thin as a thread pulled tight. She understood quite clearly that he would never say it, because he had told her so himself on a harbour wall in the dark, and the knowledge sat in her chest like a cold pebble. In the end it was Leo's bicycle bell, ringing wildly from the far end of the quay, that broke the spell, and they both stood up with a kind of relief.

On Sunday Wren sat with Aunt Dot among the roses in the sunny garden of Rose Cottage and said nothing at all about the job, though it sat between them like a third teacup. Dot, who had spent the whole of her life noticing things that other people preferred she did not, remarked quite out of the blue that Kit looked at Wren the way a sailor in a storm looks at a lighthouse. Wren opened her mouth to protest, and Dot patted her hand and said that she was old, not blind.

On Monday evening the town hall was transformed into a studio, with long tables covered in newspaper, a hundred plain white lanterns waiting to be brought to life and enough pots of paint to colour a small rainbow. Half of Salt Cove had come with brushes, aprons and strong opinions about the correct shade of blue, and Dot presided over them all from a chair like a throne. The noise was tremendous and cheerful, and the room smelled of damp paper and poster paint.

Dr Ruiz, the shy new vet whom Dot had once tried to match with Wren, arrived with his spaniel Biscuit and stood in the doorway looking for somewhere to hide. The only free chair was next to Marta, who looked up from her lantern, said hello with unexpected softness and moved over, and within ten minutes they were sharing a pot of yellow paint and both blushing furiously. Wren caught Marta's eye across the room and received, in return, a look that said she would be extremely grateful if nobody ever mentioned this.

Mr Pell painted his lantern to look like an enormous cinnamon bun, with swirls of white icing and a single glossy cherry, and held it up to the room with the pride of a man unveiling a statue. At the next table Leo was painting a fierce green dragon with such ferocious concentration that he had more paint on his ears than on the paper. Mrs Abara, who sat opposite, declared that it was the finest dragon in the history of lanterns, and Leo accepted the compliment as no more than his due.

Wren and Kit were given a table at the very back of the hall, and each of them took a lantern and turned it carefully away from the other. The brushes scratched softly over the paper, and Wren painted a wish on the inside, small and neat, where nobody could see it until the candle was lit and it glowed through. All around them the hall smelled of paint, tea and damp paper, and over it hung a strange, shared kind of hope.

Kit said gravely that the lanterns needed a rule of their own, and Wren, after due consideration, proposed rule five: no peeking at each other's wishes until the night of the fair. Kit solemnly wrote the number five on the back of his hand with the end of his paintbrush, and for a moment they were two grinning children who had been left alone with a secret. It was the first rule that either of them had enjoyed making, and Wren noticed, with a small pang, that she both longed for the night of the fair and dreaded it.

On Tuesday evening Kit tested the little wooden rafts in the shelter of the harbour, while Leo and Wren cheered from the stone steps. A single lantern, set on a raft no larger than a tea tray, slid out across the black water with a small gold light shining through its painted sides, and the three of them watched it in complete silence. It was the most beautiful thing Wren had seen all year, and it made her realise that she wanted to see a hundred of them floating, and to see them from here.

On Wednesday Kit pressed something small into Wren's palm, a brass washer threaded on a leather cord and worn smooth by sixty years of salt and vibration. It came from the Gannet's very first engine, he said, with the offhand air of a man trying hard to be offhand, and it had never once let the ferry down. He did not say that he hoped it would bring her home, but she heard it all the same, in the roughness of his voice.

On Thursday night Marta came to the flat with a green dress, a lint roller and a lecture that she had clearly been preparing for a week. She helped Wren choose the forty best drawings, ironed the dress with the ferocity of a general pressing a uniform, and made her swear never to say yes to the first thing anyone offered her. Wren swore, and meant it, and tried not to wonder what she would do if the first thing offered was exactly what she wanted.

That night Wren lay awake and tried honestly to picture herself in Barrowfield, as she might try on a coat in a shop to see whether it fitted. She saw a small flat with a view of a wall, a crowded train every morning and a great many people who had never heard of Pell's Café, and she saw no sea anywhere at all. The picture was not unpleasant, exactly, but when she tried to put Kit into it, he would not fit, and she could not bear to ask herself why.

At dawn on Friday Wren stood alone on the little station platform, with her portfolio under one arm and a cold wind blowing off the bay. Out on the water the Gannet was making her first crossing of the day, a small lit shape in the mist, and Wren closed her fingers around the brass washer until the metal grew warm. When the train came clanking in, she climbed aboard without looking back, which was the hardest thing she had done all week.

The train rattled inland for two long hours, past green fields and sleepy villages and wide brown rivers, and with every mile the sea slipped further behind her until she could no longer smell it. Wren sat with her portfolio upright on her knee like a well-behaved child and watched the countryside fade into factories, then roofs, then a great grey crowd of buildings. It occurred to her that she had left Salt Cove perhaps five times in ten years, and that she was not at all certain she remembered how.

Barrowfield station was an enormous glass cathedral of noise, with a hundred platforms, a thousand pigeons and a river of people who all seemed to be late for something important. Nobody looked at Wren at all, which she found wonderfully restful for roughly ten seconds, and then dreadfully lonely. She clutched her portfolio, checked the address on her phone for the fifth time and plunged into the crowd like a swimmer entering cold water.

Halden and Moss occupied a tall glass building with a revolving door, a shining brass plate and a doorman who looked as though he could recognise a nervous illustrator from fifty paces. Wren walked twice around the block, rehearsing her opening sentence and abandoning it each time, before she finally pushed the door and let it carry her inside. She rode to the ninth floor in a silent lift, gripping the brass washer in her pocket as though it were a lifebelt.

In the waiting room a whole wall was covered with framed jackets of famous children's books, each one a small, bright window onto a world she had once lived in. Wren recognised her favourite from childhood, a battered classic about a bear who lost his shadow, and her throat grew suddenly tight, because she had read it at Aunt Dot's kitchen table a hundred times. It seemed impossible that this was the house that had made it, and more impossible still that someone in it knew her name.

Ms Halden turned out to be a tall woman with silver hair, round spectacles and a voice like warm honey, and she greeted Wren as though they were old friends who had been writing to each other for years. On her desk, spread out in tidy rows, lay printouts of Wren's drawings, each one marked with small yellow notes in a neat, slanting hand. Wren, who had never in her life seen her own work treated with such seriousness, felt tears prick her eyes and told herself severely not to be silly.

Ms Halden tapped a drawing of Percy asleep in his tiny nightcap and laughed out loud, a delighted, unprofessional laugh that made the whole afternoon feel suddenly lighter. Very few artists, she said, could be kind and funny at the same time, and Wren managed it on every single page, which in her experience was rarer than genius and a good deal more useful. She wanted someone who could draw the sort of books that children asked for again and again, and she believed that she had found her.

Then Ms Halden slid a folder across the desk and offered Wren the job on the spot, as illustrator and art director for a brand-new picture-book list. The post came with a generous salary, a small and friendly team and an office of her own with a window, and Wren felt the room tilt gently, as it had once done in a hall full of fiddle music. It was everything she had dreamed of at the age of nine, delivered at the age of twenty-nine, on a Friday morning, in a very tall building.

There was no need to decide at once, Ms Halden said, and she asked only for an answer by the following Friday, which gave Wren a full week to weigh the matter and consult anybody she pleased. Wren thanked her three times, which she knew was twice too many, shook her hand twice, which she knew was once too many, and walked out with the folder pressed to her chest like a shield. In the lift going down she caught sight of her face in the brass wall and was startled to find that it was smiling and crying at the same time.

Wren found a café by the grey river and ordered soup, which she was far too happy and far too sad to eat. All through the meal she caught herself scanning the crowd for a quiet man in a work shirt, and each time a stranger turned round with the wrong face, her heart gave a small, foolish lurch. A tourist boat went past on the water, ten times the size of the Gannet and a hundred times less loved, and she watched it until it vanished round the bend.

Wren stood on a windy bridge and called Marta, and when she said that they had offered her the job, Marta whooped so loudly that three pigeons flew off the railings. Then Marta paused, which was entirely out of character, and asked the one question that Wren had been dodging for weeks: not what the salary was, nor how big the office, but simply what she wanted. Wren looked down at the dark water, opened her mouth to answer and found, to her dismay, that there was no answer there at all.

The journey home felt a great deal longer than the journey out, as return journeys so often do when the traveller has not made up her mind. Rain began to streak the windows somewhere past the second river, and Wren stared at her own faint reflection, at the unopened folder in her lap and at the dark green hills sliding by like a slow, damp film. For once in her life she had been offered exactly what she had dreamed of, and she found that she wanted somebody to tell her what to do.

The only evening train from Barrowfield reached Salt Cove at a quarter to seven, in rain as thick and grey as a curtain, and Wren was the only passenger to climb down onto the empty platform. The station lamps made small yellow puddles in the darkness, the sea muttered somewhere behind the houses and the whole town smelled of wet stone and seaweed. She had never in her life been so glad, and so sorry, to be standing in the one place she knew best.

At the far end of the platform, under the one lamp that still worked, stood Kit, wet to the ankles and holding a very large black umbrella over absolutely nobody. She had never told him which train she was taking, and she understood at once that he must have studied the timetable, found the single evening service and stood there, perhaps for an hour, on the off chance. Her heart did something complicated and painful, and she walked towards him as if the platform were a very long way.

Kit tilted the umbrella so that it covered Wren completely and left his own shoulder out in the rain, where it darkened steadily without complaint. He took the heavy portfolio from under her arm without a word, tucked it beneath his coat to keep it dry, and fell into step beside her down the hill towards the harbour. The rain drummed on the umbrella like a thousand impatient fingers, and neither of them said anything at all.

At the bottom of the hill, where the lane ran along the harbour wall and the wind came in off the dark water, Kit finally cleared his throat and asked how it had gone. His voice was carefully light, like that of a man enquiring after the weather in a country where he had never planned to travel, and Wren heard every effort that it cost him. The question hung between them in the rain, and she found that she would have given a great deal to answer it simply.

Wren told him the truth, because there was nothing else to tell: Ms Halden had loved her drawings, and had offered her the job on the spot, with a salary, a team and an office with a window. Kit listened to every word with his eyes fixed on the road ahead, and the umbrella did not waver by so much as an inch. When she had finished, he said that it sounded like exactly what she deserved, and she wanted, quite badly, to shake him.

Wren stopped under a streetlamp, so that the rain made a silver curtain all around them, and said that she did not know what she was going to do. She had a week to answer, she explained, and she needed every hour of it, because for the first time in her life she did not want to say yes just to make someone happy. Kit nodded slowly, as though she had said something perfectly reasonable, and his face in the lamplight was as unreadable as a closed book.

Then Kit said, in a low, steady voice that sounded as though it had been rehearsed all day, that he would never ask her to stay. It would not be fair, he said, to ask anyone to give up a chance like that for a small town, a ferry and a man who could not even say what he meant. Wren felt something inside her crack quietly, like a thin pane of ice, because it was the one sentence she had been silently begging him not to say.

At her door Kit handed back the portfolio, said goodnight in a voice like gravel and walked away into the rain before she could answer, leaving the umbrella propped against the wall. Wren stood on the dripping step with her hair soaked and her mouth open, wanting to call him back, and every word she had ever known went out of her head at once. She had always been able to say yes to anything, she thought, and now, when it mattered, she could not say anything at all.

That night Wren sat at her kitchen table and drew a line down the middle of a clean page, with Barrowfield on the left and Salt Cove on the right, like a woman balancing a ledger. The left-hand column held four sensible things, a salary, an office, a famous name and a future, while the right ran off the paper and halfway across the table, and every entry was a person, a place or a smell. Near the very end she wrote one more word, looked at it for a long time and, being a coward, crossed it out.

On Saturday morning Pell's Café was packed to the doors with market-day customers, every one of whom was pretending, with great skill and no success, not to watch Wren and Kit. Wren, who had not slept, and Kit, who looked as though he had slept even less, sat at the window table as carefully polite as two strangers on a train. Even the teaspoons seemed to be listening, and Mr Pell had been polishing the same cup for ten minutes.

Mrs Abara, who had never believed that a question could be too personal to ask, called across the café with a hopeful grin that she would like to know when the wedding would be. Every other conversation stopped at once, forks hung in the air, and Mr Pell abandoned his cup entirely. Wren and Kit looked at one another across the table, and for the first time since the whole thing began, neither of them could think of a single thing to say.

Wren stood up so fast that her chair crashed to the floor, and she said, in a voice that shook with hurt, that perhaps none of it had ever been real. Kit stared at the tabletop for a long moment, and when he answered, it was in a flat, polite voice she had not heard since the day they met. He said only two words, rule one, and in the silence that followed, the sound of the café door closing behind her was the loudest thing in Salt Cove.

The café slowly began to murmur again, in the awkward way that a room does after somebody has dropped a plate, and nobody quite looked at the man at the window table. Kit sat alone in front of his cold coffee, took the old napkin from his shirt pocket and held it unopened in both hands, like a letter he had been afraid to read. Behind the counter Mr Pell put down his cup at last, which in thirty years he had never been seen to do in the middle of a crisis.

That afternoon someone knocked at Wren's door with a small, urgent fist, and she opened it to find Leo, windblown and solemn, with a large sheet of paper held out in front of him like a petition. It was a drawing, in thick wax crayon, of the three of them standing beside a giant lantern on a beach, with a green dragon in reading glasses looking down from a cloud. In the corner, in his careful capital letters, he had written the words WREN KIT LEO AT THE FAIR.

Leo asked, with a wobble in his voice, whether she was still coming to the fair, and added that Kit had been banging things in the shed all morning, which was what Kit did when he was unhappy. Wren, who had promised herself never to lie to him, knelt on the doorstep and said that she did not know yet, but that she would look at the drawing every single day until she did. Leo accepted this with the gravity of a diplomat, hugged her around the neck with surprising force and ran off down Gull Lane before she could see his face.

Kit sat alone in the ferry shed that evening, and old Mr Pell came in carrying a flask of tea and wearing an unusually serious face. He sat down on an upturned crate and told him, with great kindness, that he was a stubborn fool, and that everyone in Salt Cove had seen how he looked at Wren from the first day. Kit stared at the floor for a long time, and then he did something he rarely did: he did not argue, and he did not hide.

Mr Pell tapped the napkin on the workbench with one thick finger and said that a rule is only a fence, and that a man who built it may climb it whenever he likes. Kit objected that fences exist for a reason, and Mr Pell replied, with unexpected gentleness, that the reason is nearly always fear, and that he ought to know. Kit had been looking at Wren, he added, as if she were the whole sea, and in all his years he had never seen a man drown from admitting it.

On Tuesday Aunt Dot climbed the steep stairs to Wren's flat, out of breath and indignant about it, with a battered shoebox clutched to her chest like a baby. She set it down on the kitchen table, untied the faded ribbon around it and revealed a hundred small, soft envelopes, all addressed in the same bold, slanting hand to Miss Dorothy Ashby. It was time, she said, that Wren learned something about her aunt that hardly anyone in Salt Cove had known for fifty years.

Dot told her about Henry Marsh, a sailor with laughing eyes who had asked her, at twenty-five, to sail away with him and see the whole world. She had been too frightened to say yes, so she had said nothing, and he had gone, and his letters had come for years from harbours with beautiful names until they stopped. She had spent half a century arranging other people's love affairs, she admitted, because it was far easier than risking her own, and all she had ever wanted for Wren was that she should stop hiding.

On Wednesday morning Leo marched up to Wren's table in Pell's Café and announced, with the solemnity of a boy about to defy the law, that he was going to break the biggest promise of his life. Kit was out on the ferry until noon, he said, and there was something she needed to see, though she must never tell him that Leo had shown her. Wren, who had not drawn a line in three days, followed him out into the sunshine without a word of protest.

In the loft above the ferry shed, where a great window opened on the whole silver curve of the bay, Leo whisked the old sail off the secret with a flourish. There stood a small driftwood desk, sanded smooth as a shell, with a groove for pencils, an edge shaped for a left elbow and, scratched in one corner by a guilty person of eight, a tiny dragon in reading glasses. Kit had made it for her, Leo whispered, for the real Wren, and he had been working on it for weeks without telling anyone, which for Kit was a kind of shouting.

Wren sat down at the desk, laid both hands on the smooth wood and felt, for the first time in a week, perfectly and completely sure. She opened her laptop and wrote to Ms Halden, without a single apology, that she would be honoured to take the job, and that she would do it from a loft in Salt Cove, where she drew best. It was the first time in her life that she had asked for exactly what she wanted, and she pressed send before her old habit could talk her out of it.

Within the hour a reply arrived, and it was only three lines long, and the third consisted of an exclamation mark and a small drawing of Percy in his nightcap. Ms Halden wrote that she had hoped Wren would ask for exactly that, that half her best people worked from places she could scarcely pronounce, and that the answer was an enthusiastic and unconditional yes. Wren read it aloud to the empty loft, and the gulls outside, who had heard everything, wheeled past the window as if applauding.

On Saturday night the whole of Salt Cove gathered on the beach as the sun went down, hundreds of small shapes against a sky the colour of peaches, each carrying a painted paper lantern with an unlit candle inside. Dot, in her brightest scarf, strode up and down the sand with a clipboard like an admiral on parade, and Mr Pell's enormous cinnamon bun glowed already beside the harbour steps. Wren stood in the middle of it all with her own lantern held to her chest, scanning every face for one particular quiet mechanic.

Wren hurried along the beach, past Marta and Dr Ruiz, who were holding hands and pretending not to be, with Biscuit the spaniel sitting between them like a chaperone. Marta caught her eye and mouthed the words you owe me a bun, and Wren laughed aloud for the first time all week, because the debt, it seemed, was about to become a good deal more complicated. At the top of the steps Dot, without a word, pointed one gloved finger towards the water's edge, where a tall figure stood alone with a lantern.

Kit stood at the edge of the water with a painted lantern in one hand and the old napkin, creased and softened by weeks of carrying, in the other. In a voice that shook only a little, he read the four rules aloud, one by one, and after each of them he said that it was broken, or that it no longer mattered. When he had finished, he looked up from the stained paper and told her that there were none left now, and that he had no idea what to do without them.

Kit said that he was not pretending, and that he had not been for a single minute since the morning she pointed at him across Pell's Café. He had never been able to say what he felt, he said, not to Dana, not to his father, not to anyone, but he was saying it now, and it was that he loved her. He would not hold her to anything, he finished, but if she wanted to hear it, he was asking her, with every word he had, to stay.

Wren told him, laughing and crying together, that she had already taken the job on one condition, that she could do it from Salt Cove, and that she was not going anywhere. They lit their lanterns together and, by the glow of two candles, each read the wish painted inside the other's: his said Ask her to stay, and hers said Be brave enough to ask. Then she said that she loved him too, and he kissed her, in public and not in the least by necessity, while a hundred small lights slid out across the bay.

By the following spring, the old napkin hung in a neat frame on the wall of Pell's Café, where Mr Pell showed it proudly to every visitor and told the story at great length. Wren worked contentedly at her driftwood desk in the studio above the harbour, while Kit hummed over an engine below and Leo drew dragons on the floor between them. Aunt Dot, passing the window, only smiled and said that she had told them so.
